speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-79, an Act respecting the provision of compensation to depositors of Canadian Commercial Bank, CCB Mortgage Investment Corporation and Northland Bank in respect of uninsured deposits be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, the legislation the Government is proposing intends to compensate uninsured depositors of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank as well as the CCB Mortgage Investment Corporation if this institution cannot resolve liquidity and other problems resulting from the failure of the CCB, and to arrange the appointment of new advisers.
Before I address the Bill more fully I want to make perfectly clear that it is not the Government's intention to set a precedent in compensating uninsured depositors in our financial institutions. We are compensating these depositors because the situation facing these two banks reflects unique and particular circumstances.
Although these two banks accounted for less than 1 per cent of the Canadian banking system they provided important support to economic activity in western Canada at a very critical time. Depositors who stayed with these banks shared the Government's view that regional financial institutions can play an important role in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as I said last week, the problems experienced by the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank reflect a set of unique and particular circumstances. The Canadian banking system is and remains one of the most stable in the world. In fact, as I indicated earlier, the assets of these two institutions represent less than 1 per cent of the total assets of the Canadian banking system.
Both banks had their beginnings in Western Canada in the middle of the seventies. Both were located in a region that was
experiencing rapid economic growth as a result of the energy boom, and both grew substantially during this period.

The economic recovery in western Canada is still fragile. The boom came in the late 1970s for western Canada, and Alberta in particular was a vibrant and buoyant market-place. It was in that environment that the CCB and the Northland were born and prospered. The bubble burst in the early 1980s when world energy market conditions and the National Energy Program depressed the economy of Alberta. Through the depression those institutions, and those who kept deposits with them, helped cushion the serious economic impact of the recession on western Canadians.
My colleagues and I consider this legislation a matter of the highest priority. It is a high priority because of the importance that we on this side of the House place on easing of financial and economic problems of municipalities, small businesses, charitable organizations, credit unions, labour unions, hospitals, colleges and particularly individual Canadians. These problems are a direct result of the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank.
The major elements of this Bill will come as no surprise to this House. They have been the subject of some considerable discussion over the past few weeks. The circumstances surrounding both the Canadian Commercial and the Northland Bank have been put forward to this House on many occasions and most recently in a statement made here last Monday.
Let me say again that the action our Government took last March regarding the CCB was on our Government's recognition of regional financial institutions and also in recognition of the importance of the CCB to the western economy. We also based our decision on the international circumstances last March.
Our Government examined all the options at that time and in consultation with two provinces and six chartered banks we went forward with the support package. These facts are well known to the House.
Let me now also outline the key elements of this legislation so we can all speak from the same point of reference on the matter.
First, this Bill would authorize the Government to compensate all the depositors of the two banks who maintained deposits in excess of the $60,000 amount protected through the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
Second, the Government is proposing that the uninsured depositors covered under the legislation be paid in two installments. The First installment would be paid as quickly as possible following Royal Assent to this Bill and would repre-

October 7, 1985
Depositors Compensation
sent 60 per cent of the total amount payable to each depositor. The balance, 40 per cent of the outstanding deposits, would be paid on April 1, 1986 through a post-dated cheque which each depositor will receive with the initial payment once the legislation has been adopted by Parliament and given Royal Assent.
As Hon. Members may be aware, the payments in respect of insured depositors are made by the CDIC under the CDIC Act. The payment of the uninsured portion of the deposits is to be made under Bill C-79 following the coming into force of the Act.
Accordingly, all that is now required is that the Act be passed by Parliament. The ruling of the Manitoba court has no effect on the process of compensating all depositors.
Depositors will receive full compensation for amounts on deposit as of September 1 but they will receive no interest between September 1 and the date of actual payment. This decision reflects a careful balance between the Government's desire to compensate uninsured depositors in this particular case and the need to ensure continuing market discipline with respect to financial institutions.
This Bill also provides for the offsetting of deposits where possible. In such situations, depositors who have outstanding loans with the banks may have their cash payments reduced by the amount of those loans. This action is normal practice in a liquidation.
That is the essence of the Bill, Mr. Speaker. I would urge Hon. Members to give the elements of this Bill their full consideration. However, I would also urge them to do so expeditiously.
There will be many questions relating to the circumstances surrounding the demise of the CCB and the Northland Bank. I would like to remind all Members that those circumstances surrounding the failure of both banks are currently being examined by Mr. Justice Willard Estey. Therefore, today we are talking about the imperative to help those organizations and individuals across the country who have been adversely affected by the closure of the two banks. The debate today should focus on the elements of this legislation. I ask Hon. Member opposite to put the needs and concerns of Canadians above partisan politics so that this House can meet those needs in a fair and expeditious manner.
Over the past few weeks, Members of the House have voiced a number of concerns with respect to the legislation the Government has proposed. I want to address those concerns because I believe that once concerns like these are laid to rest, we can move quickly to approve the Bill.
Hon. Members opposite have demanded that the Government release the names of the depositors who will be compensated under the terms of the legislation. I have said on many occasions that the privacy of individuals must be protected and that the laws of this country do not appear to permit the publication of this information.
They do in a bankruptcy.
To violate the confidentiality of the Bank Act would put all depositors in Canadian institutions at peril should any Government in future wish to get access to and publish that data.
Not true. This is a unique situation.

That is the law, and despite the fact that the broad based nature of the depositors would probably help demonstrate that the Government is doing the right thing, the Government must respect that law and principle.
I promised the House that 1 would provide a detailed breakdown of the classification of uninsured depositors which should meet all reasonable requirements for information on the nature and amounts of the payments that will be made. Let me state now those categories of depositors and the value of their uninsured deposits. I shall table in the House as soon as the French version is available a list of the categories and the amounts of deposits as of August 31, 1985. In the meantime, let me tell the House of some of the highlights of that document which we expect to have available shortly.
With regard to the Canadian Commercial Bank, credit unions and credit union centrals and $67,840,043; municipalities, $41,059,682; school boards, schools and post-secondary institutions, $3,102,928; religious organizations, $2,267,241; charitable organizations, $1,499,763; labour unions, $6,510,856; and hospitals, $5,192,054.
With regard to the Northland Bank, uninsured depositors included credit unions and credit union centrals to the extent of $61,921,647; municipalities, $40,707,740; school boards, schools and post-secondary institutions, $216,461; religious organizations, $4,970,452; charitable organizations, $13,172,093; labour unions, $331,496; and hospitals, $4,716,434.
What about the other $600 million?
It will be in the document, Michael.
How much will foreign banks receive? What about Peter Pocklington, is he on the list?

The total amount of these uninsured deposits, the amount being requested under the terms of this legislation, is $414 million in the case of the Northland Bank and $532 million in the case of the Canadian Commercial Bank. The numbers which I have just quoted suggest $946 million for uninsured deposits in the two institutions. However, the liquidator anticipates about $140 million in set-offs, which would result in the Government compensating uninsured depositors for approximately $806 million. As some set-offs are likely to be subject to further legal consideration, the $875 million appropriation figure in the Bill assumes the exercising of only one-half of the anticipated set-offs. Therefore, I believe that the $875 million figure is an overestimation of what will be required.
I would like to emphasize as well that the appropriation of $875 million requested in the Bill will not be the final cost to
October 7, 1985

the Government or the taxpayer. That cost will be lower by the amount of recoveries from liquidation of the assets of the two banks.
The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation has already begun payments to insure depositors of the CCB and is starting to make payments to insured depositors of the Northland Bank. Insured deposits for the CCB and the Northland together total $275 million and $318 million respectively. These funds will be obtained by borrowings by the CDIC which will eventually be recovered, with interest, through recoveries from the liquidation and through premium payments made by financial institutions which are members of the CDIC.
Once this legislation has been approved by the House, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will act as the agent for the Government of Canada in connection with payments on uninsured deposits. Application forms will be mailed as quickly as possible by the CDIC to all those eligible under the Bill. Depositors may complete these forms and return them to the CDIC which will then issue the two cheques. Depositors will have until April 1, 1986 to file such applications to the CDIC.
I have described some of the classifications of depositors who will be paid under the Bill. These are deposits within the meaning of the definition of "deposits" in the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. This includes demand deposits, term deposits and U.S. dollar accounts.
The public policy underlying the Bill applies only to depositors-those who have entrusted their money to the banks. Other creditors are more analogous to creditors in a conventional bankruptcy and will rely on the liquidation process. The legislation does not include shareholders of common or preferred shares or debentures, nor does it include participants in the support package which was arranged for the Canadian Commercial Bank last March.
As well, the funds advanced by the Bank of Canada to both the CCB and the Northland are not covered by this legislation. Those advances, some $1.3 billion to the CCB and $500 million to the Northland, are secured by assets of the banks. The six chartered banks and the two provincial Governments which participated in the support package will have, together with the Government of Canada, the right to claim a pro rata share of the proceeds of the realization of the assets of the two banks once the affairs have been wound down. As holders of subordinated debt, the Governments of Canada, Alberta and B.C. will not receive a share from the realization of the CCB's assets.
Under the terms of this Bill, the depositors, in return for compensation of their uninsured deposits, will assign to the Government all their uninsured rights to a share in the assets of the banks following liquidation proceedings. In effect, the Government of Canada will become the major uninsured depositor.
I would like to be able to advise the House of the final cost to the Government of this compensation package. At this stage, though, it is too early to determine what final recoveries
Depositors Compensation
might be. I do not want to tie the hands of the liquidators by engaging in speculation in the House today. Every effort is being made, with the co-operation of the liquidators and the other creditors, to ensure that the sale of the assets of the two banks is undertaken in an orderly manner in order to obtain a maximum value from them.
The decision to provide compensation to the uninsured depositors was not a decision which we made without careful attention to all the factors relating to this issue. 1 believe very strongly in the importance of the deposit insurance system and in the necessity for investors to act responsibly in choosing where to place their money. So the support we are proposing today should not be interpreted as blanket insurance that similar support would be forthcoming in the event that a financial institution faces difficulties in the future. That is why we will move to increase the powers of the federal regulatory authorities and to change the CDIC Act so that the deposit insurance system will have the financial resources necessary to protect Canadian depositors of modest means.
Over the period since the completion of the CCB support arrangement, the Inspector General of Banks has supplemented the resources of his office through the engagement of individuals outside of the Public Service on a contract basis. Following implementation of the support agreement, two bankers were engaged as special representatives to supervise the arrangement.
Subsequently, three recently retired bankers were engaged to conduct an examination of the CCB loan portfolio. Another retired banker was engaged to assist with the review of the Northland portfolio.
Currently, the Inspector General of Banks is finalizing arrangements to bring under contract a number of active and retired bankers to assist in the regular program of bank inspections now in progress. All this followed, Mr. Speaker, a 30 per cent increase in the Inspector General's staff over the course of last year.
At the same time, the Inspector General will be seeking the authority to increase the permanent resources of his office. I have already indicated, Mr. Speaker, that the Government intends to introduce legislation very shortly to increase substantially the power and authority of our regulators. We will continue to do our best as supervisors, regulators and policy makers to ensure that our financial institutions meet the highest possible standards. These changes will ensure that we have the best regulatory system in the world.
As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, we are proposing to compensate the uninsured depositors of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank because the situation of those banks reflects unique factors. These depositors stayed with the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank as an expression of confidence in the viability of regional financial institutions which we were all supporting. When I say "we", Mr. Speaker, I include the major chartered banks and

October 7, 1985
Depositors Compensation
two provincial Governments in addition to the federal Government.
We are paying these depositors as well because of the serious economic impact which would result, especially in western Canada, from forcing municipalities, credit unions, charities and small businesses, to absorb the total loss of all their deposits in excess of the $60,000 limit insured by the CDIC.
I have already indicated to the House some of the classifications of the depositors, and all Hon. Members can imagine the impact on these organizations and the individuals they serve and employ if the Government were not taking the action proposed today. Many of them would be in serious financial difficulties. We are talking about the domino effect which insolvencies have with lay-offs, permanent loss of jobs and all of the problems which go with business failures of that sort.
The plight of some municipalities which invested their surplus cash in the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank has been well documented in the media. In this part of the country we have heard of the situation facing Kanata which has been forced to defer many of its capital projects and provide only essential services until the status of its deposit has been resolved. Kanata is not the only municipality in this situation. What were we to do in the circumstances, Mr. Speaker? Should this House be telling those municipalities, "Sorry. Tough luck. Raise your property taxes or go to your provincial Government"? Surely we have a responsibility to them, having participated in the March support arrangements.
Hon. Members opposite are openly critical of the decision of the Government to include the deposits of foreign banks as part of the terms of this Bill. However, it would not be a responsible action on the part of this Government to protect only certain kinds of depositors. What kind of signals would we send to the international financial community if we were to take that kind of action? I suggest that any refusal to indemnify foreign depositors would have been seen as a major breach of trust, both at home and abroad, and our banking system would become truly insular if we paid off Canadian depositors while not paying off non-Canadians.
Therefore, the Government had to weigh the impact and the criticism from the other side of the House which it might receive because of our decision to pay all uninsured depositors against the widespread difficulties which would occur across the system had there not been such indemnification.
I mentioned at the beginning that it is the Government's hope that the House will move speedily to pass this Bill through all stages so that it can send out the cheques as soon as possible. The organizations and individuals affected by this problem are very concerned. Over the past few weeks, the CDIC has received over 400 calls a day from people who want to know what their status is and when they might expect to receive their compensation. Many people have written directly to me because they or their companies are facing serious problems.
Let me give a few examples. A small construction company which put its partial payment for a job into a 30-day certificate is now in the position of being unable to pay its workers and sub-contractors and will have to start laying off employees. I have also received a letter from a small western Canadian business which employe 25 individuals. The uncertainty around the status of the company's deposits and the timing of the payments means again that the business must start laying off its employees. I mentioned the plight of the Municipality of Kanata, and it is not the only municipality caught in these circumstances.
I could go on and talk about calls from individual Canadians to many Members of the House and to the CDIC. These are ordinary businesses, ordinary organizations employing ordinary Canadians and engaged in standard investment practices. They deserve the support of the House and its assistance and they need speedy consideration of this Bill so that they can get their lives and their companies back to financial stability again.
In conclusion, let me repeat what I said in the House in May when all Members agreed to the speedy passage of similar legislation with respect to Pioneer Trust. As a Government, we are committed to the responsible management of the affairs of this country. That is a heavy responsibility and one that we take seriously. It is one that carries with it the necessity of making difficult and complex decisions. We have made those decisions and we have concluded that our responsibilities include the protection of depositiors faced with the unique and unusual circumstances surrounding the fate of the Canadian Commercial and the Northland Banks.
I would like to thank Members opposite in advance for their co-operation in this matter. Believe me when I say that they are not helping the Government, they are helping thousands of Canadians who have been caught up in this regrettable matter.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it was just a Monday morning speech, but that was not a very spirited defence of this legislation. 1 can understand why.
As a matter of fact, I am surprised that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is not in his place today either to present the Bill or to hear his colleague, the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall). He has general responsibility for the banking system and for the financial system in the country. It has been delegated, to a certain extent, to the Minister of State for Finance. However, a billion dollars is a billion dollars and the Minister of Finance should have been here to address the issue and hold himself accountable to Parliament for that issue.
In March, the Government put together a bail-out for the Canadian Commercial Bank. Those of us on this side of the House were skeptical but we-

But you supported it.
October 7, 1985

We supported it and we agreed with the Government on the basis of ironclad solutions that the bail-out would be successful and render the bank solvent and viable again. We supported the Bill on the basis of that assurance.
We were told that it was a temporary problem that was a result of a few bad management decisions. Upon review of the history of that bank, it turns out that it was more than a few bad management decisions. That bank was badly managed from its inception.
We were also told that it was an isolated incident. I want to put on the record what the Minister of State for Finance told Parliament at that time. I am quoting from Hansard on March 25. She said: "We are satisfied that this bank is now a viable bank, that it will be profitable in the future, that we will be repaid as will other members of the support group out of the future profits of the bank". That was an undertaking. That was a clear statement. It was not conditional. It was not hedged. She went on to say: "This particular problem was triggered by something that happened within the bank's loan portfolio in California, which then of course created problems with the organization as a whole". That was the position of the Minister at that time. It was not just the western Canadian economic position or the National Energy Program. It was the bank. The fact happened to be that the bank invested very heavily into Texas and California, into loans directed at the oil and gas industry and directed at the real estate in those states. That had as much to do with bringing down this bank as did the economic situation in western Canada.
Then she went on to say: "Indeed the matter must be clearly explained so that Canadians understand that this is an isolated incident due to very particular circumstances, an incident that poses no threat to the integrity of the banking system". Of course we now have a companion piece with the Northland Bank; that is about how isolated the incident was.
We agreed that the $255 million bail-out should be passed by Parliament after being told repeatedly by the Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance that the problem had been solved and that there would be business as usual. We also supported the Bill at that time and the bail-out then because we wanted, as did the Government, to restore full confidence in our banking system, a banking system which, despite these set-backs, remains in our opinion among the strongest in the world. We also gave a vote of confidence to the Government at that time because we were giving a vote of confidence to our regional banks and a vote of confidence in the western Canadian economy. Regional banks have been chartered under previous Liberal administrations because we recognized that western Canadians were becoming fed up with having to come to Montreal and Toronto all the time for a loan beyond a certain loan authorization limit. They wanted banks with head offices in British Columbia, Alberta and other parts of western Canada, so that they would not have to board an airplane, come to eastern Canada and lay their
Depositors Compensation
problems before a remote credit institution. I believe that has helped to decentralize and to bring our banking system closer to the people of western Canada. That is why we supported the original bail-out in March. However, the undertakings which were given to Parliament and to us were pretty flimsy and very fragile, indeed. Now, just six months later, we have been told that not only one bank is in trouble, but that two banks have collapsed and that it will cost Canadian taxpayers $1 billion plus to reimburse uninsured depositors.
It is absolutely mind-boggling. We now know, on the basis of evidence before the Finance Committee, evidence given by chief executive officers and senior officers of the chartered banks, that at the time the Government brought the bail-out to Parliament, it did not know the facts. Despite the pleas of the senior officers of the chartered banks to look at the loan portfolio of the Canadian Commercial Bank, neither the Inspector General, nor the Department of Finance, nor any government official, went into that loan portfolio. The chartered banks said to the Government on a Friday night: "Give us a weekend. We will lend you some people, 40 or 50 experts, to go into the loan portfolio of the bank and to examine the assets of the bank". That was not done. That offer was refused. The Government flew absolutely blind. It did not do its homework. It had no idea of the state of that loan portfolio and, as it turns out, instead of $255 million, those loans were sour to the extent of $600 million to $800 million. The bail-out was inadequate. If we are going to bail out, then bail out; and get to the bottom of the boat.
Like Maislin.

The Hon. Minister ought to know that this matter is far more serious; it goes right to the confidence of our banking system. She should know that well and not retort in a flippant way, which has really characterized her whole performance on this issue.
The chartered banks volunteered their experts and they volunteered an analysis. All that was refused. We had a situation where the Government was flying blind. On the day before Parliament reopened in September, I called it "amateur night on the Rideau". We on this side of the House were conned at that time. We relied on the Ministers for their undertaking that this bank would be rendered viable once again. We were conned. The chartered banks were sucked in. The Government did not know anything about what it was doing. It was absolute, sheer negligence. None of the homework had been done. It was really "amateur night on the Rideau". Apparently a letter of comfort was also provided to the other chartered banks which participated in the deal. It guaranteed the survival of the bank and guaranteed that the banks would get their money back. In purchasing the proportionate assets of the Canadian Commercial Bank, the banks were guaranteed by the Government that they would be treated as depositors. We will have to look into that more closely as we get into committee.
As I said, it now turns out that about a third of the loans of the Canadian Commercial Bank were rotten, that $255 million

October 7, 1985
Depositors Compensation
were thrown away and that the taxpayers' bill is at least $1 billion. The Hon. Minister said this morning that, in addition, the Governor of the Bank of Canada authorized $1.3 billion against the Canadian Commercial Bank and another $500 million to $600 million against the Northland Bank. She said that those were fully covered by the assets of the bank. We will wait and see. I hope the Minister will eventually report back to Parliament as to what are the set-offs and as to what is the final bill for the Bank of Canada. It ought to be added to the bill.
What we have here is a shaking of confidence in our system by reason of the incompetence of the Government. As a matter of fact, that confidence has now been shaken to such an extent that the market is now in control. Ottawa has lost control. Only the resignation of this Minister and the resignation of the Minister of Finance will restore confidence in the country that there are Ministers who devote their full attention to the banking system, who supervise it with care and who pay attention to the deals negotiated. Only that type of action by the Government, giving the supervisory force a fresh face, will restore what has been lost.
Hear, hear!

The Minister of State for Finance solemnly assured us in March that no other banks were in trouble. Then, seemingly out of the blue, on September 1, she tied the problems of the Northland Bank to those of the CCB. She announced the appointment of curators for both banks. In that September 1, 1985 press release she gave Northland, "a limited time period to seek to reorganize its affairs or amalgamate with another financial institution". That was the kiss of death of the Northland Bank. Once she linked the Northland to the Canadian Commercial Bank, which had then gone into liquidation, investors, depositors and other financial institutions were given a clear warning by the Minister that the Government did not really have any confidence in the bank and was giving it just a limited period of time.
Given the complete irresponsibility of the Government in the CCB collapse in not fully examining the books of that bank, how can we now presume that a thorough examination of the books of Northland was undertaken before it, too, was declared no longer viable?

Mr. Speaker, this is unprecedented. The President of the Northland Bank said before the TV cameras that he had the impression the Government wanted to force the Bank to close, although he felt the Bank could have survived.
We are also informed that a letter delivered by hand to the Minister on September 6 informed her of a rescue operation set up by the Bank, and that the Government has yet to reply to this letter. This raises some pretty obvious questions: Did the Minister actually carry out a thorough examination of the situation at the Northland Bank? Was the Bank really insolvent? To what extent did the Government's intervention contribute to the Bank's collapse? Why was the Canadian Commercial Bank given the benefit of the doubt in March and why was the Northland Bank denied that benefit in September?
We feel the Government committed a serious mistake by giving both banks the same treatment, and it has failed to give us a satisfactory explanation for its decision to act in this way.
These issues ought to be looked into, not only by Mr. Justice Estey in the course of his inquiry but also by a committee of the House. Considering that the courts have now decided to grant the Northland Bank a reprieve, should this Bill even be before the House? Should we postpone this Bill until the courts have had a chance to rule on the matter?
Why, for instance, did the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) not attend the negotiations back in March? Why did the Canadian Commercial Bank decide for itself which loans would be examined by the bail-out group?
According to some reports, officials of the Canadian Commercial Bank got rid of their own shares in the Bank before the Minister's announcement that the Bank would be bailed out, which would have depressed the value of these shares.
[DOT] (U40)

Questions have also been raised about insider information and secret meetings. Why was no evaluation of the Canadian Commercial Bank begun until three months after the bail-out? I have already said that, on the basis of evidence given to the committee, the homework was not done and that the books of the bank were not examined before the Government came to Parliament with the $255 million bail-out package. Even then it took three or four months before George Hitchman, a former senior executive of the Bank of Nova Scotia, was finally commissioned by the Government to look at the books of the bank. It was shortly after his report was received by the Minister in late August that on September 1 the plug was pulled by the Government.
Why was a report of February 14 from the Federal Reserve Board in San Francisco not forwarded by the Inspector General to the Minister? Why did she not see that the Federal Reserve Board system of United States has serious doubts in February about the viability of the bank and its subsidiary, the Westlands Bank of California? These warnings from the American banking system were ignored by the Government.
We are now being asked to authorize the expenditure of nearly $1 billion of taxpayers' money. I venture to say, from what I was able to gather from officials who wanted to speak quietly about the matter, that the Minister of Finance was not too keen about the bail-out in March, and neither was the Minister of State for Finance. They both went to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), who said that there was no way he was going to allow the first bank since 1923 to go bankrupt under a Conservative administration. He operatee without the facts. He did not ask for them and, if he had asked, he would
October 7, 1985

not have got them from the Ministers because they did not know the facts. If the story is correct that the Ministers did not want to support the bail-out in the first instance and were over-ruled by the Prime Minister, they may still be in their places because the Prime Minister owes them one. Otherwise it does not make any sense.
This is the first bankruptcy of any bank since 1923. The Ministers absolutely failed to do the elementary homework of looking at the books of the CCB, and they are still around with the price tag of $1 billion to the Canadian taxpayers and another $2 billion outstanding by way of the Bank of Canada. This Parliament is now being asked to authorize nearly $1 billion of taxpayers' money to be turned over to a group of anonymous depositors. The Minister said this morning that this was not going to set a precedent.
However, the people of Canada are entitled to ask the Government if in future all depositors and investors will be bailed out. Is there no meaning any more to the interest rate structure and the market system? Depositors were paid a higher rate of interest because the market presumed that there was a greater risk and now that differential and margin means nothing. Is there now to be an implicit guarantee of the Government of Canada that it will bail out future depositors in any difficulty in any financial institution in the country? The people of Canada are entitled to ask that question.
We know that there are some legitimate claims by native bands, pension funds, municipalities and credit unions. They have been in touch with us. The Minister has read out some global figures. All of these institutions were misled by the Minister in March, by the Prime Minister when he authorized the deal, and by the Minister of Finance in categorical statements before this House. On the basis of those statements, reinforced, it must be said, by statements of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, credit unions, smaller municipalities, and school commissions across the country deposited with this bank for short and medium terms. I suppose that is the moral justification, if there be any, for the Government bailing them out. The incompetence of the Government misled $ 1 billion worth of depositors.
Hear, hear!

During our debate on this Bill, Mr. Speaker, we will want to examine the difference between short-term demand deposits and medium-term debentures. A good many of the credit unions and municipalities were persuaded to go in by way of debenture. If the Bill passes Parliament we will want to ensure that there is some equity between deposit holders and debenture holders despite the rather vague reference in the Bill to security under deposits.
We have repeatedly asked the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance for the names of all the depositors of the Northland and CCB. They tell us that under the Bank Act it is illegal to provide the names of depositors and that the confidentiality of deposits is fundamental to the banking system. That may be so, but as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), set forth very
Depositors Compensation
clearly in questions to the Hon. Minister, these institutions no longer fall under the Bank Act. According to the terms of the Bank Act, when a curator and liquidator are appointed, the Winding-up Act takes precedence and under the Winding-up Act the liquidator is entitled to know the list of all creditors and debtors. Among the creditors, of course, are the deposit holders. More than that, not only is there no legal bond in our view, it is absolutely unprecedented for the people of Canada, through the House of Commons and Parliament, to be asked to disburse $1 billion without knowing where a cent of it is going.
Hear, hear!

We take the position that we will not support this Bill until we know who is being bailed out. This quarter of the House will not authorize any blank cheques from Parliament. How much of the money which we are being requested to authorize is going off-shore, to foreign banks, and to other banks in our own system? How much is going to class A and class B banks? How much is going to wealthy individuals who took a chance of a higher return? Is this the real reason we are not getting the names? Who are they? I think it would be a fascinating list. I am sure the Minister would be intrigued to give us that list. She has a bit of an enigmatic smile on her face. I think we have reached her a bit. Only she and the Minister of Finance know, and I am sure the Prime Minister has taken a look at the list. I have heard of buying a pig in a poke, but never for $1 billion. We believe that it is high time the Government was honest with the people of Canada. [Translation]
The Government is asking us to make the same mistake it made in March, to spend millions of dollars of taxpayers' money without knowing all the facts, especially the most important fact which is: Who is going to receive this money? Who are the anonymous invisible beneficiaries of the Government's generosity? Are they friends of this Government?

In fact, by tabling this Bill, the Government is saying to Canadians: "Trust us, we know what has to be done. There is nothing to fear. Just trust us." Well, we trusted them in March, and six months later, not one but two banks have gone bankrupt!
Canadians, and I say this through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Government, Canadians believed you a year ago when you said that social programs were a sacred trust. And then, in your very first Budget, you attacked the Old Age Security pension and family allowances.

Canadians trusted this Government when it said that it would revise the patronage system. That was one of the great ones. Twelve hundred names later, when every thirsty Tory had been to the trough, not only directly but through uncles, aunts, brothers, and brothers-in-law, when they had satisfied their thirst for patronage, we heard a sanctimonious statement by the Prime Minister and some reference to the committee of the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). So where is the reform; where is the trust? Canadians trusted this Government when it said there would be improved standards for Ministers. What are the standards? It is asking for trust here, for a blank cheque of $1 billion. We in this House are entitled to ask, where is the trust? We are losing about $1 billion in taxpayers' money, plus whatever the Bank of Canada is unable to set off against the $2 billion that the Bank of Canada had advanced. That should be reason enough for both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance to turn in their resignations. I believe they contributed to a loss of confidence in the system.
Where is the new morality in this Government? The former Minister of National Defence goes to a questionable bar and he resigns. The former Minister of Fisheries allows rancid tuna on the shelves, but the Prime Minister sticks with him until the Minister contradicts the Prime Minister. There is the morality. The former Solicitor General calls into doubt the whole administration of our justice by having a secret, clandestine meeting in the Chateau Laurier with a potential accused who happens to be the Tory Premier of New Brunswick, and he stays. The former Minister of the Environment, now the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) undermines the credibility of our fight to protect the environment by emasculating her Department, then she takes extended business trips to Europe on questionable grounds, five hours work for a ten-day trip. She stays. Now the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance blow $1 billion of the taxpayers' money through sheer incompetence, and they both stay on the job. That is the new morality; that is the new credibility; that is the new standard of behaviour for Ministers.
Last Wednesday night in which the Tory Government almost refused the emergency debate and almost put into jeopardy your authority and the authority of the Chair, Mr. Speaker. It was only those on this side of the House who rescued the House Leader by reminding him that if they had
not voted against allowing the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) to bring in his motion he would be in effect sapping the confidence in the Speaker and in the Chair of the House.
You all voted for it.

Last Wednesday, after we insisted upon a registered vote from every Member on the other side, to restore confidence in the Chair, Member after Member on that side of the House got up and blamed past Liberal Governments for this fiasco. How absurd can one get.
You just did.

How feeble an excuse. In March the Minister of State for Finance did not talk about past administrations. She said then the bank's difficulties had to do with loans into the American market in the southwest and California and Texas. Now the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance are blaming past Governments. We never had a bank go bankrupt under our administration, Mr. Speaker.

Oh, oh!

The question is not why
the Canadian Commercial Bank found itself in trouble. It found itself in trouble because of world economic conditions but primarily because of bad management.

The issue before this House is, why did this Government come in March with an inadequate picture, with an inadequate factual background, has not done its homework, misled the Parliament of Canada and misled the Canadian people? That is the real issue.

-I am saying CTVs Question Period on September 20, the Minister of State, even after admitting to the reporters who were interrogating her that the decision to bail out the bank was made on false or at least inadequate information, even though she admitted it was based on inadequate information, said that she would do it again. in the ability of this Government to supervise the system. The system has taken over. The market has taken over. Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of my Party to speak unequivocally against the Bill that has been introduced today. It is very clear from this Bill and from the related lack of action by the Government over the summer on whose side the Government is. When a group of municipalities, people in the industry and workers from Vancouver Island asked for some $22-million worth of assistance to provide concrete jobs for those in the wood-producing sector, the Government said no.

In the Province of Quebec, when they have problems with their factories or in their communities, the Government once again says no.

When prairie farmers who have experienced the worst drought in several decades asked for speedy assistance, the Government said no. However, when uninsured depositors, most of whom are wealthy individuals or corporations, came to the Government, then within 48 hours the Government indicated it was prepared to give them millions of dollars and shortly thereafter billions of dollars. It is clear to us on whose side the Tories are. It is time that the Tories started listening to the people of Canada rather than the bankers of Canada.
Having heard the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) say that the Liberals were not going to give, in his words, a blank cheque to the Government today, I would say that it is too bad that the Liberals did not take that position last March. If they had taken that position last March, we might have been able to stop the Government from carrying on with the incredible bungling that has occurred since then.
The Leader of the Opposition says he is not going to sign the blank cheque. None other than the Leader of the Opposition was the co-signer of the blank cheque last March. If the Liberals have learned a little bit since then, perhaps the people of Canada will reap some benefit from that wisdom.
I listened with care to what the Leader of the Opposition had to say. He did not say that the Liberals would oppose this Bill in principle. He indicated that after they received a list of the names of uninsured depositors, something which this Party has showed great concern over in the last week, then they will probably support the Bill.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Who said so?

Of course he did not say so. I know how the Liberal Party works, however. The Leader implied that they would do again in October what they did last March. When
the bankers call, the Liberals will come to their assistance just as fast as the Conservatives.
The average Canadian, whether a farmer on the Prairies, a steelworker in Hamilton or a bank clerk in the Minister's own riding, probably finds it hard to envisage that which the Minister throws around so casually; namely, $1 billion. To give it some concrete reality, I would say to the Minister that what she is now proposing to put as a charge on the taxpayers of Canada is equivalent to all the groceries required for one week for every family in Canada. It is equivalent to writing off the personal income taxes of every income tax payer in the Provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland combined. It is equivalent to an amount of $80 being paid by every individual taxpayer. As well, after making a rough calculation, $1 billion would be enough to send every man, woman and child in my constituency a cheque for $10,000. In other words, we are talking about a lot of money that this Government is now wasting because of its own mismanagement.
That the Government is wasting $1 billion is bad enough, but we should put this in the context of the other expenditures that have occurred in relation to this mess. The total net effect of this fiasco could be in the neighbourhood of $3 billion. That is the equivalent of three tax-free years for every person in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. The other examples to which I referred a moment ago could also be multiplied by three.
Let us add to the $1 billion bail-out the following costs: $135 million was spent in the original bail-out which occurred in March; $1.8 billion was advanced by the Bank of Canada to Northland and the CCB between March of last year and September; and another $420 million is likely to be added to the taxpayers' charges because this amount will be provided by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to the insured depositors, and as the Minister well knows, this tab is likely to be picked up by the taxpayers because the CDIC is currently running at a deficit of $1.2 billion. We are talking not only about a $1-billion fiasco but quite conceivably about a $3-billion fiasco.

Mr. Speaker, the irresponsibility and superficiality of the two Ministers are as great as the amount this affair is going to cost the taxpayer. Just consider for a moment: the bail-out operation for the Canadian Commercial Bank was put together in just 48 hours, back in March, and at that time the Ministers refused an offer from the chartered banks to make a detailed study of the Canadian Commercial Bank's financial situation, which would have taken only two or three days. And during the summer, the Ministers failed to attend some very important meetings on the subject. The Ministers did nothing when the chartered banks, including the banks taking part in the bail out, withdrew $360 million from the Canadian Commercial Bank during the summer.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the President of the Northland Bank accused the Government of sabotaging the Bank's restructuring operations. The truth of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that we have here a monumental Government fiasco.
October 7, 1985



I want to indicate briefly why we are against this course of action. There are already provisions in place in legislation making it possible, through the CDIC, to compensate depositors of up to $60,000. Those beyond that were taking a risk and they knew it. Surely, the Minister who practises the efficacy of the market-place in such situations ought to be practising what she preaches. Those depositors above the $60,000 level were making those deposits to obtain additional interest for moving in the non-insurable category. They were taking risks. They knew what they were getting into. I say that, overwhelmingly, people and institutions in that category, whether they be chartered banks, other financial institutions here or banks in the United States, rich individuals or other groups in the Canadian community, were taking risks. It is inappropriate to come to the taxpayers of Canada now and ask them to bail them out.
Hear, hear!

That is our view in principle.
A bad precedent will indeed be created no matter what the Minister says today. If we are to say now that all uninsured depositors with deposits over $60,000 will be bailed out by the taxpayers, then what type of effect will this have on management decisions in our banking institutions in the future? Will they be prudent in the future or will they simply say: "We had better not risk our capital on that sort of speculative venture in California, western Canada or eastern Canada"? Not at all. What the Government is doing by this legislation is encouraging the opposite of prudence. What the Government will be saying to banking institutions is: "There is no longer a distinction to be made between insured and uninsured depositors. Go ahead and take whatever risks you want; be however irresponsible you want to be. The people of Canada will pick up the Bill". I want to emphasize at this point that it is the people of Canada involved here, not some abstraction known as the Government of Canada or some political Party. We are saying that this is a bad example to set. We will not support it for that reason.
In recent days in the House we have given a great deal of attention to the fact that we will be giving almost $1 billion to a group of individuals, corporate entities or municipalities whose precise names we do not know. I thought it was a great bit of unintended irony for the Deputy Prime Minister who, in the House on Friday, in answer to questions on a different matter, underlined the important principle that the people of Canada as taxpayers have a right to know where their money is going. I say to the Minister responsible for this Bill that if they have a right to know in some categories where their money is going, then they surely have a right to know where the money is going in today's circumstances when the Government is proposing to pay $1 billion out of some taxpayers' pockets into other taxpayers' pockets. They have a right to know where that money is going. That is the important principle.

In the House last week the Minister replied that she could not supply that list because there is a tradition embedded in Canadian law, in fact, in the Bank Act, which says that names of uninsured depositors have to remain secret. How quaint. She does not hesitate as a Minister of a Conservative Government to change another tradition, namely, to use taxpayers' money to bail out uninsured depositors for the first time in Canadian history. She will do that but she will not similarly change this other old tradition with respect to the names of uninsured depositors being released.
To make a point I have made in the past, she cannot have it both ways. She cannot say that we will change one tradition but we are unprepared to change another, that is, with respect to the withholding of names of uninsured depositors. We are saying, quite apart from other points about this Bill, that it is absolutely fundamental to the whole notion of parliamentary democracy that when taxpayers are footing the bill they ought to know where their money is going. If uninsured depositors such as foreign banks, rich individuals or corporations inside or outside of Canada are to be paid off, then we want a list of those names.
I noted some ambivalence on the Government's part on Friday in replying to questions on this matter. In making this proposal we say there are two options. First, there is the option provided by the Conservative Chairman of the House Finance Committee, and also the President of the Toronto Dominion Bank, both of whom have said publicly that the list of all depositors, uninsured as well as insured, should be made known. We would go for that. Second, if the Government is giving this money away and if the Government will use taxpayers' money to pay off uninsured depositors, then, at the very least, it can provide us with a list of the names of the uninsured depositors.
I have made the points I want to make in this debate for my Party today. I want to conclude with these observations. We want a list of names. We do not want it in abstract categories, as I have said. We are opposed to this Bill in principle. This Government was elected on a mandate just over a year ago which promised constructive change. This Government promised to build a new atmosphere of optimism for ordinary Canadians in all regions. Since it has come to power it has increased taxes on the average Canadian by almost $1,000. That figure is before we take into account the impact of this Bill. The Government has ignored the increasing concerns of unemployed Canadians. It has not been prepared to support financially the legitimate concerns of working Canadians, whether they be prairie farmers, those in the logging industry or fishermen. The Government has made it clear whose side it is on. That could not be demonstrated more clearly than through the Bill which is before us. The Conservative Party is quite clearly not living up to its mandate to help the ordinary Canadian. It is living up to its own private agenda with respect to aiding the wealthy and the powerful.

We are opposed to this Bill. Unlike the Liberals, we will vote against it, whether or not we receive a list of the names. We think it is bad for Canada.

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate to support the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) and this important and essential measure to provide compensation to uninsured Canadian Commercial Bank and Northland Bank depositors.
The one and only purpose of this Bill is to repay uninsured depositors, although it is obvious that Members of the Opposition intend to raise many other irrelevant issues which do not relate in any way, shape or form to the legislative measure now under consideration.
I intend to focus my simple remarks on the sound reasons why this measure is both necessary and warranted, as well as on the reasons why the Bill is of utmost significance to depositors and the economy of Western Canada. It is quite clear that Parliament must endorse these repayments without delay. Indeed the issue we are debating has to do with the savings of individuals, the cash flow which small-and medium-size businesses so badly need, the temporary deposits of municipalities, small and big alike, the cash reserves of religious and charitable organizations, and many other such deposits.
Surely all Hon. Members must realize that any undue and irresponsible delay in the consideration of this Bill will have wide-ranging and disastrous consequences. For example, if a businessman were unable to cash in an investment certificate redeemable this month when he needs it to pay suppliers, subcontractors or his employees, the shortage of cash facing the businessman would have an impact on several other branch plants and their staff. This problem could be the source of unexpected and rather heavy additional expenses that are harmful to small businesses and might even lead dependent companies to bankruptcy.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I urge all reasonable Members of the House not to delay for ever the adoption of this Bill. I
October 7, 1985

suggest it would be quite unfair to seek to score doubtful political points in a spirit of shortsighted partisanship by trying to take advantage of the fact that many Canadians would thus find themselves in an economic bind.
Still, some important questions must be raised in their proper context. Some people mention the basic principle whereby it is bad policy to provide financial compensation to the depositors of the institutions, in addition to the payments they receive from the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation on the first $60,000. They gratuitously add that the insurance money is enough and that we ought to reject all other applications for additional assistance, no matter what the mitigating circumstances might be or without any consideration for the impact on the business community.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State (Finance) was very clear and altogether unequivocal in supporting the existing deposit insurance system. I might remind Hon. Members that last June a private sector committee chaired by Mr. Robert Wyman of Vancouver published a detailed report on ways to strengthen Canada's deposit insurance system. The Minister is actively seeking ways and means to consolidate our deposit insurance scheme and especially to reinforce the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation's ability to protect Canadian depositors of modest savings.
The Government feels that this protection system is fundamental, that it is a crucial and essential feature of our financial system. The bill before us, therefore, should not be viewed as weakening in any way Canada's deposit insurance system.
The Minister has clearly indicated that the Government's decision to grant additional support to the depositors in question had been made in the light of the very special circumstances under which deposits had been made in these institutions and that this additional help is in no way an indication that the Government would take similar action if and when other financial institutions duly insured under the CDIC failed in the future. I should like to remind the hon. members of the reasons why the Government has deemed it necessary and essential to take this major decision and to go beyond the normal limit provided for under our deposit insurance scheme. I suggest that the Government's decision was based on two major considerations. First of all, the very serious financial and economic difficulties which would result if the uninsured deposits were not compensated by the Canadian Government. The sustained profitability and, in some cases, the very existence of a number of small and medium-sized businesses, organizations and other smaller depositors depended upon funds frozen in both these financial institutions.
As I said earlier, a major company unable to recover most of the funds it had deposited in one of these banks might possibly fail, which might in turn cause a number of secondary firms in business with this major company to fail.
Depositors Compensation
It has been repeated on many occasions that both these banks are relatively small. Their cumulative assets account for only 1 per cent of the total assets of our banking system. But everything is relative. The fact remains that within the regional context in which they operated, they played major roles indeed and were major institutions. I urge, therefore, all hon. members, while dealing with this Bill which is to provide for the compensation of all uninsured depositors, to consider the regional problems which would result in the economy of western Canada if the Government failed to act to ensure a proper treatment of the depositors.
In this regard, I should like once again to go over the detailed breakdown list of uninsured depositors of these two banks which was provided by the Minister of State (Finance). I will state the total amounts at stake for each category of depositors.
Religious and charitable institutions, for instance, have nearly $22 million invested in uninsured deposits in the two banks. The credit union movement in western Canada, which is the western equivalent of our "caisses populaires", has about $130 million in deposits of the same type as the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. Corporations generally hold over $141 million of these deposits, while individuals and non-incorporated businesses hold some $32 billion. The great majority of individuals, or 88 per cent of them, had uninsured deposits under $60,000 in addition to the first $60,000 already insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. The provincial Governments had deposits of nearly $145 million, while small and large municipal administrations had deposits of some $82 million. As for the hospitals, their deposits only amounted to about $5 million.
Obviously, these are the total amounts deposited in both banks. I have only tried to summarize a few details included in the report given today by the Minister of State for Finance. However, these figures show eloquently how significant the impact would be if we did not approve quickly the bill now under consideration.
The second major factor which influenced the decision by the Government concerns the events of last spring and last summer, especially as regards the position of the Canadian Commercial Bank after the Government and its financial partners, the major Canadian banks, implemented their support program to provide assistance to this bank last March.
With such a program, the Government and its financial partners showed their support for the concept of regional financial institutions. As agreed, the Bank of Canada provided the required cash, first to the Canadian Commercial Bank, and later also to the Northland Bank. Depositors who kept their deposits in these banks thus showed their confidence in the action and the moral endorsement provided by a responsible Canadian Government. Unfortunately, despite these well-

October 7, 1985
Depositors Compensation
designed support measures, it finally became obvious that the two banks were unfortunately no longer viable. However, if we consider all the circumstances existing at the time, I believe that any reasonable person will agree that the Government acted responsibly by helping the depositors who had shown their confidence in both regional institutions and who also had confidence in the moral support they had received from the Government.
Mr. Speaker, I am not minimizing the cost of these support measures. Payments to insured depositors will total about $875 million, or perhaps somewhat less when we know the exact amount of the liabilities of the depositors with these banks. In addition, the amounts produced by liquidating the assets of both banks will reduce the total cost.
Uninsured depositors will also incur significant costs. Indeed, their deposits have stopped earning interest since September 1. In addition, they will receive nothing as long as this Bill is not implemented; afterwards, as official trustee, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will act as quickly as possible to make the first payments, amounting to 60 per cent of the deposits and interest earned until September 1. The second cheque of the CDIC covering the difference of 40 per cent of the deposits will be sent with the first payment, but it will be postdated April 1. In view of all these facts, I once more urge all the Hon. Members to allow this Bill to receive quick passage and not to delay unduly compensation of the depositors by debating at length matters which are irrelevant or only indirectly related to it.
I am not denying the crucial importance of some of these questions. However, they will be settled by other means and we shall have every opportunity to examine them in two ways. First, Mr. Justice Estey has been given the most general terms of reference possible to investigate all the circumstances surrounding the bankruptcy of these two unfortunate banking institutions. I am certain that all Canadians can trust him to make a detailed, careful and in-depth examination of these very important issues. The haste with which he has immediately set down to work is a most encouraging indication of his wish to solve the problem as quickly as possible.
Second, strengthening the system for regulating and monitoring our financial institutions raises major questions. The Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) has indicated how the Office of the Inspector General of Banks had already found extra resources by calling upon a number of retired bankers to help complete some urgent tasks he had to do last summer. The Minister has also announced that the Government intended to take legislative action as soon as possible to give increased powers to the regulating bodies, in order to guarantee the stability of our Canadian financial system, and in term that of all Canadian citizens generally who are directly or indirectly involved in this country's healthy financial climate.
Third, the working paper on the reform of this country's financial institutions, that is the green paper submitted by the Government refers to significant changes. This green paper is now being considered by the Standing Committee of the
House. It might be useful, Mr. Speaker, to add in that respect that the committee is on schedule, and last week there was a sitting of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade, and Economic Affairs to which members of all parties were invited. It was with great pleasure that we enjoyed the cooperation of the New Democratic Party, however we must point out the noticeable absence of the Liberal Party from those three-day discussions that were held last week.
If Members of the Official Opposition had attended, Mr. Speaker, maybe their Leader would have made quite a different speech today. I therefore give you my word that this second item of the green paper discussion is very important, and it is unfortunate that the Official Opposition did not assume its responsibilities in delegating some of its expert Members capable of playing an intelligent part right where the work has to be done, that is in the Standing Committees.
If I referred to those other questions that will be investigated and considered from a legislative point of view, it was because I wanted to make it quite clear that this Government is not today closing the door to public debate on any of those questions. In fact, we are hoping for a comprehensive and an in-depth study of the facts. Many aspects of that complex issue have to be debated. But I would like once more to urge Hon. Members to realize that the legislation should not be subjected to a protracted debate on those other irrelevant issues, however important. Let us examine the Bill with an objective eye, keeping in mind that we must act quickly so that the depositors do not have to wait unduly for the funds they so urgently need and to which we feel they have an imprescriptible right.
Mr. Speaker, on all those questions we believe that, although the matter is not sub judice, there are two ways of discussing the Bill, and all matters which are relevant thereto or which indirectly, involve this legislation. There are two forums: first, the Standing Committee on Finance, which is now studying in a very positive way the matter of financial institution reform, and, second, a judicial one, where we have a judge with very broad terms of reference was appointed to make an inquiry using all the means left to his discretion. Therefore, with those two points in mind, we feel we must ask the House to approve the legislation within the shortest possible time frame, in order to avoid possibly irreparable harm to small and medium-sized business in Western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address the amendment which was moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). The amendment makes it clear that we on this side are not ready to proceed without having further information about the people to whom this very large sum of money will be paid out. The Government is asking for $865 million to be paid to the uninsured depositors, that is, those people who have over $60,000 on deposit in the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Westland Bank. Let us not forget that those with deposits of $60,000 or less will be fully compensated by the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation. We are talking about people who are not entitled to be compensated for over $60,000 who will have received their full $60,000 back. These people, whether individuals or businesses, will be asking the Government to pay them moneys in excess of that. The Minister wants us to agree to these payments without knowing where they are going.
This is absolutely unprecedented. Treasury Board rules require that payments be disclosed in the Public Accounts of Canada. The Bill itself requires these people to complete an application in a specified form. We will know these names in any case. What on earth can the Government hope to achieve by hiding the names from us now since they will be made public sooner or later? The taxpayers of Canada have a right to know where this money is going. It must be absolutely unprecedented that an amount of almost $1 billion be paid out without public disclosure, although a large number of people will know because the application forms will surely have to be handled by officials at varying levels of seniority in many government Departments.
When we return to the circumstances under which this bail-out was put together, we end up with some very serious questions of trust. The Government assured us, as the Official Opposition, that it was essential to bail out the Canadian Commercial Bank. It assured us of this in private meetings and asked for our agreement to let a Bill go through all stages of the House with remarkably little information. We were assured this as well on the floor of the House.
Let us look at some of the assurances given, assurances which were absolutely unequivocal. Starting on March 25, the Minister in her own speech stated that with the bail-out, the Canadian Commercial Bank would be viable and that it would continue to make a contribution to the economy of western Canada. Assurances were also given by the same
Minister that, with the bail-out which was arranged on March 25, the bank could be expected to be profitable and that some of the moneys put in by the Government might in fact be recovered. Afterwards we found that it was all based upon hope of some kind. The Minister has repeated many times in the House that the decision was based upon "the best information available". I am referring to the original decision in March to put together a rescue operation of $255 million. It was supposed to make the bank viable and profitable and was supposed to get the taxpayers' money back to them eventually. Yet on September 1, the same bank was put into liquidation.
If we look back at the sequence of events, it becomes more and more difficult to accept the Government's word, and I say that with great regret. This is why we could not possibly consider accepting on faith that the moneys would be paid to depositors and that the depositors were all hospitals, municipalities, school boards and so on.
Let us look at what happened. Early in the morning on March 25, we were told that over the weekend the Government had concluded negotiations with six banks and two provincial Governments to provide a major infusion of funds to the Canadian Commercial Bank, which otherwise, we were told, would not have been able to open its doors that day. We were told then that the CCB had sought assistance from the Government on March 14 and that prior thereto there had been no indication of the seriousness of the bank's problems. Later we found that the Government really did not know. We have had the banks concerned say that they had to make their decision based upon a segment of information provided only by the Canadian Commercial Bank, and that when they offered their staff and expertise to go in and make a full examination, they were refused. One bank president said that the only reason given for the refusal was that the Canadian Commercial Bank did not want competitors examining its assets. This was the first time a bank had failed in 62 years. When a bank comes hat in hand to Ottawa asking for $255 million, I have great difficulty understanding why it is in a position to dictate its terms and say that we may only look at the information offered, not at anything more. I cannot understand why the Government would accept that. We have asked these questions in the House and have received no answers.
Afterwards we learned a number of specific things in committee. We agreed to the passage of the Bill because we accepted the Government's word. The Official Opposition should be able to accept the word of the Government. Then we went into committee and found that there were many other problems. For example, we found that the bank was greatly over-extended as a result of imprudent lending practices. The committee found much of concern in the accounting policies of the bank and in its information disclosure. We have increasingly discovered, as a result of information before the committee and elsewhere, that the Government made its decision with inadequate information. We found that the Government did not seek out the opinion of CCB's external auditors in March before deciding to put in $255 million. The Government did not consult the minutes of the bank's own audit committee.
October 7, 1985

The Government did not attempt to inform itself about the February 1985 report of the American regulators on the Canadian Commercial Bank's U.S. agency. As I said, the Government did not insist upon a full examination of all assets but accepted the portion or segment of information provided by the Canadian Commercial Bank as a basis for decision.
At the same time as the Finance Committee was hearing these disquieting facts, and after the initial report of the Finance Committee was released, the Government continued to issue assurances about the effectiveness of the bail-out and the viability of the Canadian Commercial Bank. It was known throughout the summer that the Bank of Canada was providing considerable amounts of money to the Canadian Commercial Bank, obviously because large amounts were leaving the bank. Nevertheless, with the Government's assurances still ringing in our ears, the announcement on Labour Day of the appointment of curators for the Canadian Commercial Bank and for Northland came as a shock to most Canadians. Why had the Government put $255 million of taxpayers' money into a bank rescue, only to preside over its failure six months later? Clearly, confidence in the Government's original decision was badly misplaced. Obviously there were things which the Government had not known when it put together the bail-out.
When the House resumed in September, we asked questions, but our questions have not been answered. Today the Minister offered to table something to which she has referred for weeks, a partial list of categories of depositors. That will not meet our needs. We need full disclosure and exactly who are the depositors for which the Government is now showing a lot of concern, although it showed no similar concern for the shareholders.
Many of the shareholders are little people. I received a poignant letter from a 70-year old man who sold his house and on the advice of a broker invested all the proceeds in the Canadian Commercial Bank following the bail-out, when the Government was telling us that the bank was viable. This man has lost every penny. There is no concern for the shareholders. The shareholders include the pension plans of many Canadians. Air Canada, various teachers' groups and railway workers had invested in the shares of the Canadian Commercial Bank. They have lost every penny.
The Government has an obligation to explain why it is bringing in special legislation to pay out almost $1 billion to depositors whose names we do not know, while it is refusing to consider any special assistance for shareholders whose names we know. We know who some of the depositors are because they have chosen to identify themselves. The municipalities of Kanata, St. Catharines and Toronto have chosen to identify themselves. I have also received letters from municipalities in western Canada; they have made their position known. However, who are the depositors who have not been identified and for whom the Government wishes special legislation to pay out many millions of dollars of taxpayers' money without disclosure? We must have those names.

Mr. Speaker, statistics show that 49 per cent of all fires and 90 per cent of all fire
deaths in Canada occur in homes. One-third of those who die in fires are children. Such a grim record prompted fire departments from across Canada and McDonald's restaurants to launch Canada's first national family fire drill as part of National Fire Prevention Week, October 6 to 12.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and I know it is of concern to him. For many disabled Canadians the use of wheelchairs is absolutely necessary. Will the Government move now to remove the sales tax on wheelchair replacement parts?

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly delighted to know that we have made changes on some things, but the point I want to make is that for many people a wheelchair is an absolute necessity. Canadian savers are now being seriously penalized as a result of the bankruptcy of a Canadian bank among others because... the officials of the Tory Government of Canada have ill advised and badly protected them.
