Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Hon. Member who was, of course, a member of the Government Party prior to the last election and who has served in this House for some time and whose interest in these areas of financial responsibility is well known.
My question is this. The new Government has certainly made many errors in this particular area. However, it inherited the Inspector General of Banks; it inherited an office of the Inspector General of Banks which was woefully weak and understaffed; it inherited in fact a can of worms from the old
Government which had allowed the shenanigans of the Canadian Commercial Bank to go on, the playing around, the chairman in California, the shoddy loans, the consorting with people of the reputation of Leonard Rosenberg and so on. I would simply like to ask the Hon. Member where she and her Party were and where her Government was when seeds of the problems, which will cost the taxpayers $1 billion if this Bill goes through, were being sowed under the former Government. Why on earth were not members of the Liberal Party at that time speaking up and saying that something has to be done to make these banks act responsibly?

Mr. Speaker, what is at issue in this debate is not the conduct of the banks per se but the conduct of the present Government. No Liberal Government ever let a bank fail, neither did any Liberal Government pump in taxpayers' money to rescue banks. It is no secret that in a similar situation what the previous Liberal Government had done was to ask other banks to arrange a merger or to put their own house in order. I have raised this point more than once in this House. We have never seen fit to put in taxpayers' money to rescue a bank. This Government did, and did it without looking at the facts.
Furthermore, the Government not only put in taxpayers' money to bail out the bank in March and assured us that it was then safe, but in September, only six months later, it is presiding over the failure of the bank and asking us to agree to use more taxpayers' money in order to compensate those people who were led to keep their money in the bank between March and September by the assurances of the Government.
In this debate we deal with the conduct of the present Government not previous Governments.

Mr. Speaker, I disagree with the Hon. Member in that last statement. As the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) says, if the previous Government had made sure that the office of the Inspector General of Banks was functioning properly-he only has eight people working for him, for heaven's sake-if he had a full support staff-the State of New York has 300 people in such an office-if we had a situation where we had the proper staff, does not the Hon. Member agree that this kind of thing would not have happened?
The Hon. Member said in her speech this morning that this Government was not aware of what was going on until March 14 when the CCB people came to the Government for help. Surely to goodness, when we look back into what has happened, proper inspection would have indicated that this bank was in trouble a long time before that, and the blame lies right in the pocket of the Member opposite, in the previous Government's purview.

I said this morning indeed that the Government told us on March 25 that it had no indication the bank was in difficulty prior to March 14, but in fact, in response to further questions in the House, it emerged that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had had a discussion with the Inspector

While I think the Hon. Mr. Speaker, my question to the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) is a reflection of the earlier questions regarding the lack of regulation and supervision that occurred and resulted in the collapse of these banks. Can the Hon. Member explain why, over the years, the office of the Inspector General of Banks had only eight inspectors to do the job of supervising and monitoring the entire banking system? Why was there any hesitation in expanding that office when the banks themselves paid for the Inspector General of Banks and all the people he hired? Why did the Government not go out of its way to expand the size of that office when it was not costing the taxpayers of Canada a red cent?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know why additional staff was not added to the office of the Inspector General of Banks at a time when, following the revision of the Bank Act, the number of banks in Canada greatly increased. There was a rather obvious case to be made for increasing the number of inspectors. However, I still say that that is not relevant to the present situation because there was information available from the Inspector General of Banks which the Government did not look at in making its decision.
Furthermore, no matter how many inspectors there are or what information they can provide, political decisions are the final responsibility of Ministers. The Ministers chose to make a decision based upon very little information. Even if we accept that because of the small size of the staff in the Department of the Inspector General the information presented to the Ministers was inadequate for them to make a responsible decision, we must not forget that the banks concerned offered staff and resources to make a fuller appraisal before the final decision was taken and their offer was refused.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words about

Bill C-79, the famous banking bail-out Bill. It has been referred to in all sorts of ways but I think the people of Canada have now begun to appreciate the seriousness of this situation.
If the last few weeks have been any indication, I suspect that the people of Canada have become rather confused by the Government. There have been statements one day saying one thing and then retractions the next day. For many weeks, we have heard Ministers and other members of the Government say one thing, only to have to reverse their positions within 24 or even 48 hours. By and large, people are beginning to wonder to what extent they can believe what the Government says.
Today we are debating the $875-million bail-out Bill. This is just the first instalment in a long list of pay-outs. I do not want anyone to get the impression that only $875 million will be shovelled out of the taxpayers' sack into the bail-out operation. Much more is yet to come.
Regarding the changing points of view of the Government, do we not all remember when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) rose in the House of Commons to say that the Canadian Commercial Bank was a viable bank, and after he said that the bank failed? The Governor of the Bank of Canada phoned the offices of The Globe and Mail on a number of occasions to say that he had full confidence in the Canadian Commercial Bank, that it was a viable operation and that he would stand behind it. As a matter of fact, at a meeting of the Finance Committee held on May 19, he said that he had a high regard for the management of that bank. Since then, we have come to understand just what kind of management the Canadian Commercial Bank had. Certainly some very questionable practices were being used.
The Inspector General of Banks, time and time again, said that the Canadian Commercial Bank was indeed a viable Canadian bank and that no one had anything to fear. Of course, as we all know, the bank failed. Unfortunately, my good friend, the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDou-gall), was required on a number of occasions to rise in the House to say that the Canadian Commercial Bank was a viable operation in western Canada and that no one had anything to fear. Of course, the bank failed.
We cannot have a viable institution on Monday and a failed institution the next Monday unless the people to whom we look to supervise and monitor the bank did not do so. It cannot have happened unless Governor Bouey and all the other players did not know that about which they were speaking when they made those public commitments.
What has become very clear is that this is an example of group-think. The Minister of Finance, the Minister of State for Finance, Finance Department officials and senior bankers all got together to say that they were wonderful, sophisticated people with a great deal of banking expertise, that the Canadian Commercial Bank is viable and that they would all agree to that. What they forgot to do was their homework. They forgot to ask if they had the facts that enabled them to make those comments. As we now know, they had incomplete information.

We are told, and of course we do not know the facts, that the Inspector General went to the management of the Canadian Commercial Bank, a management we now know is highly suspect in terms of carrying out prudent bank management practices, and asked for the facts. The management provided the Inspector General with facts that were not facts but fiction regarding the viability of the assets of the Canadian Commercial Bank.
We did not have the facts. Since the Minister of State for Finance is an experienced Bay Street financier as is the Minister of Finance, I do hope that this is not a reflection of those on Bay Street. Hopefully others are not making decisions regarding Canada's banking and financial future based upon incomplete or even no information.
I would like to make one suggestion today. I suspect that we will hear from members opposite regarding a retraction or explanation of this. We are now dealing not only with the Canadian Commercial Bank failure but the Northland Bank failure. I suspect that one of the reasons for the Northland Bank's failure was that when the Minister of State for Finance made her announcement after the Labour Day weekend, she said that the Government would rescue the uninsured depositors as well as the insured depositors not only of the Canadian Commercial Bank but of the Northland Bank. I suspect that a great many people took that as a very clear message that the Northland Bank was in serious difficulty. If they had not removed their funds already, they certainly did so after hearing that announcement. In a sense, we could say that the Minister of State for Finance began the slow demise of Northland Bank which was trying to rescue itself in the troubled western economy.
I would repeat what the President of the Northland Bank himself said. He called a press conference and said that the Government of Canada was sabotaging western banks. He said that it was not interested in providing assistance to get the Northland Bank back on its feet. Just the other day, one of the directors of the bank said that they were considering suing the Government of Canada because it had not given their proposals a fair hearing. This is a very serious set of allegations.
If the President of the Northland Bank and one of its major directors is saying that the Government of Canada did not do what it could to rescue this ailing western institution at a time when it was experiencing serious difficulties because of the problems in the western economy, that is a very serious case. I assume that the inquiry being carried out by Mr. Justice Estey will bring this out into the open.
The people of Canada have become rather confused by the antics of those on the government benches in the last few weeks. I suspect a great many people are scratching their heads. For as long as I have been a Member of this House, I can recall hearing members of the Conservatives Party prefacing their remarks with the belief in a free market system. They said that they believed in free enterprise and in the invisible hand of the market-place to direct decision making. They said that they believed in the discipline of the market-place. When the previous administration provided bail-out money to ailing
corporations it said that this action must stop, that market discipline must prevail if we want to see a decent economy unfold. What has become extremely clear is that the comments about the free market which are directed at the small business sector, farmers, ranchers, fishermen or Canadian individuals does not hold when it comes to banks. When banks get into trouble they are not allowed to go under. They do not even have the opportunity to go under because the Government steps in to rescue them. It is not like any other bankruptcy where 40 cents, 60 cents or even 70 cents is paid on the dollar-in this case 100 cents will be paid on the dollar. The Government of Canada has made itself the laughing stock of the financial community of the country.
I encourage Hon. Members who sit on the Government benches to stand in their places and say who they believe are recognized financiers in our country who think this move is a good example for the financial community to have placed before it. I do not think we will find anyone who will say that. I believe it was the Chief Executive Officer of the Bank of Montreal who could not help himself from laughing in front of the television cameras when asked: "What do you think about this bail-out?" He said: "I cannot believe it. We cannot believe we are being bailed out at 100 cents on the dollar. We were thinking of writing off those deposits, but the Government of Canada in its wisdom is going to bail us out." The banks could not believe it.
It must be recognized that what we have here is a direct repudiation of the free market-place. What we have here is reward for failure. In other words, the message which has gone out is that if you are an imprudent lender and if you run a sloppy management system with your bank or trust company, do not worry about it because the Government of Canada will come in and rescue you. What kind of message is that to send out to the investment community of Canada and abroad? We are saying that pay-offs for incompetence is the rule of the day. We are telling these investors: "You are an incompetent banker, do not worry because the Government of Canada will stand behind you." I do not think that is the type of message the Government of Canada ought to be sending out at this point in time.
I say that $875 million, which is the amount of money involved in Bill C-79, is only the down payment-it is only the beginning. The Government has already paid out $60 million which some folks may have forgotten. That is what was paid out in the original bail-out scheme. We will also pay out the $60 million which the banks paid out in the first rescue package. Those banks have letters from the Government saying that their bail-out money is to be considered on the same level as a deposit. As a number of bank presidents have indicated, they are expecting a full return on their original bail-out contribution, which is another $60 million. Then, of course, there is the sum of $450 million in the CDIC which is part of the insurance plan to bail out those depositors who have $60,000 on deposit or less. It is obvious that that sum will come from the taxpayer of Canada in the short term. Then,

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in support of Bill C-79. In view of the urgency among uninsured depositors of the Canadian Commercial and Northland Banks to receive the payments which this Bill would authorize, I do not intend to unduly prolong this debate. It is important that the Bill come to an early vote and be sent to a legislative committee for detailed consideration.
I think it is important, however, to emphasize just how vital it is to western Canada that Parliament should act promptly on this legislation. There are some people who argue that we should reject this proposal, that these depositors should be left to sink or swim. The image that comes to mind is that of the ocean liner whose captain refused to stop and put out lifeboats to rescue the crew of a foundering fishing boat.
There are also those who feel that the names of the banks' depositors whose deposits exceed the insured limit should be revealed to all and sundry prior to this Bill being debated. I wonder if those who advocate such a revelation would also like Canadian income tax returns published in book form? The
privacy which a depositor expects with regard to his or her banking arrangements is just as important, in my view, as the privacy accorded to an income tax return.
I do not think that it is discounting the importance of the deposit insurance principle when we recognize that there are particular circumstances which had to be considered in the case of the failure of these two banks. The Government should be commended for its willingness to stop and pay attention to the problems raised by these bank failures and to show concern for economic dislocations which these developments threatened in western Canada.
Anyone with a first-hand knowledge of how business operates will appreciate the danger to a business should a large part of its funds be tied up in another institution or lost in the failure of a bank. Some businesses cannot survive the shock and go bankrupt even though they are innocent third parties which deposited their funds in good faith. Moreover, bankruptcies can have a domino effect, hurting still other businesses, supplies and employees. Even if the business depositor manages to avoid bankruptcy, it is still highly likely that her or she will incur very substantial costs in terms of lost funds and unforeseen expenses.
We must recognize clearly that it is not possible for the federal Government to come to the rescue of everyone who is hurt by bankruptcy. Moreover, the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) has made the important point that we are not establishing a blanket policy of rescuing uninsured depositors in the future event of failure of financial institutions belonging to the Canada Deposit Insurance system.
However, we cannot ignore the magnitude of the problem that has been created by the failures of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. Granted, they were not major players on the national banking scene, but they did play a very significant role in the economies of the western provinces. The potential losses to uninsured depositors, estimated at some $875 million in this Bill, would have an impact in the western business community that we simply cannot disregard.
The figures that were provided by the Minister of State for Finance show just how large that impact could be if we do not act. In the two banks there are 437 business corporations with uninsured deposits totalling over $140 million. Small unincorporated businesses have another $4.7 million at stake. However, the potential problem is far wider than those figures alone indicate. Over 750 individuals had a total of some $27 million in deposits not protected by CDIC. Religious and charitable organizations stand to lose more than $21 million; hostpitals $4.7 million; school boards and other educational institutions some $3.3 million and labour unions close to $7 million. The list goes on and on. The credit union movement has a very large amount at stake, nearly $130 million in the two banks. Municipal governments, some of them in eastern Canada, stand to lose over $80 million in uninsured deposits and provincial governments stand to lose close to $145 million. That is still only a partial list of the amounts involved. It is obvious from these figures that we are dealing with a very

substantial problem which, due to its very size, demands special consideration.
The Government has stated a policy of supporting and promoting the development of regional financial institutions and I commend it for this approach. Regional institutions can fill a very real need in their own areas. In the case of depositors in these two banks, their deposits were a vote of confidence in a regional financial institution. There can be no doubt that one consideration which we must keep in mind is the question of confidence in other financial institutions. That confidence could be damaged if we decide that uninsured depositors in these two banks must absorb losses in the amounts I have just indicated.
There is just one culprit in this whole affair, Mr. Speaker, and that is the infamous National Energy Program which came down in 1980. These two banks were born during a buoyant economy in the West. If they had been able to hold on until the steadily mounting benefits of the Western Accord had reached a level to sustain them, this whole affair might never have happened. How were western Canadians to know that the main source of that buoyant economy was to be raped by the machinations of the Liberal Government in 1980? I personally would not like to feel that the future of other regional banks in our country is jeopardized by this unhappy affair. It was brought about, without any doubt whatsoever, by the actions of an eastern oriented and anti-western regime which wanted for itself the hard-earned profits of western innovation and determined effort.
This Bill deserves the support of this House, but what is more important is that this support should not be delayed. It has been argued that adoption of the Bill should be stalled until Mr. Justice Estey completes his inquiry. Nothing has been advanced to suggest that the issues to be examined by that inquiry have any relevance whatsoever to the question of reimbursing these uninsured depositors. It is misleading to suggest otherwise.
Let us consider the question of reimbursing these depositors on the merits of that issue alone. The issues which Mr. Justice Estey will be examining are important in themselves and the Government has ensured that there will be the widest possible inquiry. Surely, however, the question of whether or not to reimburse the depositors is quite irrelevant to the inquiry. To delay the Bill on those false grounds would be a mistake. The only result would be to add to the uncertainties and costs facing the uninsured depositors. No payments can be made until this Bill becomes law. Prolonged delay of this Bill would simply add to the depositors' costs in the form of interest earnings foregone on their funds and extra costs incurred in borrowing the necessary interim funding. I therefore urge all Hon. Members to recognize their responsibilities and allow speedy passage of this legislation which is so vital to so many businesses, organizations, and individuals in western Canada and elsewhere.

Let private enterprise, in an unfettered way, proceed to take risks. The Member says that this is a different situation because the amount of money is so large. Well, suppose the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce should find itself in the same situation. My God, the risk would be huge. Would she then argue that it is the East and we therefore should not do it? What principle will one apply? She says that we should bail out those who are uninsured. Where is the principle of insurance involved here? There are all kinds of situations in this world where people are not insured for a variety of things. I think that many of us can identify with the homeowner who has 10 children and is uninsured. I think that most of us would be far more sympathetic to furnishing the money needed to rebuild and re-establish a home for a family in that situation than to placing money in the hands of those who ought to be sophisticated enough to know that there is a danger of losing. How does one ensure prudent investment if there is a vague assurance by the Tory Government, which is so clearly identified with free enterprise, that even imprudent investment in the last analysis is deserving of a reward?
I ask the Member to please elaborate on what principle she has identified herself with. What principle motivates this free enterprise party of which she is a member in this particular situation? How does she preclude a future situation in which the same kind of bail-out will occur? Tell me why, again in terms of this instance, it is not reasonable to identify those who are going to receive the money whereas in bankruptcies in every other similar situation, where they only get part of the money that they would have lost, they must be identified.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Wind-sor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) obviously does not understand the value of regional banking. To compare a large major bank such as the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce to a small regional bank in western Canada is to indicate that you have no idea of what the West has been through. I had the opportunity in 1980 to come to Ontario to try to explain to some of the people here what the effects would be in western Canada if the National Energy Program went through. There was high employment not only in the West, but right across the country. The Member does not seem to realize that the West does need regional banking. We need banks that will take care of small businesses. We need banks that will take care of private individuals. We have banks which will look after hospitals and municipalities. Even municipalities from Ontario were investing in our banks because they cared about the small person. This is why regional banking is so necessary. I am not pitting the east against the west. I am saying exactly what happened. If we had had a decent energy program, these banks probably would never have fallen.
It is very interesting how people can rise and criticize now. Obviously the regulatory system has failed to adapt to changes in the banking system over the last eight or ten years. The Inspector General will simply require more authority and power to go in and review all operations of all banks. We will require more inspectors and tougher audits in order to keep the banking system straight.
I support the Minister of State for Finance in that she put forth a Green Paper to review the banking system. Hopefully we will move forward on that, so that there will not be another disaster in western Canada or in eastern Canada. We are one nation and we stand together.

People who trusted your Government.

I see the Hon. Liberal Member shaking his head. There would never have been a bank failure in the West if it had not been for the national energy policy. That was the beginning of it. Mr. Speaker, over the course of the next 15 minutes to 20 minutes, I hope to put this debate into references which the average people on the street can understand. Frankly, there is a great deal of confusion in the minds of the Canadian public about what exactly the Bill is supposed to do and about the bail-out package. This comes as no surprise to me, or to many Members of Parliament. Many people do not even understand the basic concept of what is a billion dollars. Each day during Question Period Members of Parliament, in an attempt to get average Canadians to understand the sum of a billion dollars, use the term "one thousand million dollars". Part of the problem is to make average Canadians understand that amount. That is complicated by the fact that there is a great deal of confusion on the part of average Canadians about what the Bill will do.
What is the difference between the rights of shareholders and the rights of depositors? That may well be understood by some Hon. Members of the House, but I do not think that it is well understood by the majority of Canadians. If they began to understand some of the definitions, then we could begin to focus the debate as it should be focused. What is at the heart of discussion today is not so much the fact that a bank collapsed; at the heart of the discussion is the trust issue. Fundamental to the way in which the House of Commons operates, we must have a degree of civility and a degree of trust between both sides of the House. That trust factor was broken in this debate by the Government front-benches several months ago.
I should like to bring into the debate the chronological series of events which occurred last spring so that average Canadians can begin to understand why we in the Opposition at this stage, now that we have had the collapse of a commercial bank, are taking our position. Back some time prior to March 25, in other words, in the months of February and March 1985, a degree of concern was raised by inspectors in the banking system as to the viability of the Canadian Commercial Bank. I would assume at that stage that those inspectors would report to the Bank of Canada, namely to Mr. Bouey, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, and indicate that they had a great deal of concern about the commercial and financial integrity and viability of the CCB. In other words, warning bells would sound. This is what inspection systems are all

about. Therefore, the inspection system was operating under normal conditions at that stage. Once the Governor of the Bank of Canada was handed a report by his Inspector General, he had no choice but to report to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), who is the Minister responsible in the House of Commons for the way in which the Bank Act is to be administered. He takes the political responsibility.
Let us for the first time in this debate separate the two responsibilities. There is an administrative responsibility which is in the hands of the Governor of the Bank of Canada and his officials, and there is a political responsibility for the banks which rests with the Minister of Finance. In this case, as we did in previous Governemnts, because of the work-load on the Minister of Finance the position of Minister of State for Finance was created. I would also assume that the events which transpired in late February and March, 1985, indicated that the Minister of Finance, who was preoccupied at the time, no doubt, with consultations in order to bring forward his first Budget on May 23, indicated to his Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) that he wished her to take responsibility for shepherding the problems of the Canadian Commercial Bank through the various stages for which the Government had responsibility.
I suppose it is going to be up to the Estey Commission to determine exactly what were the prime reasons for the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank. I doubt very much if Mr. Justice Estey is going to comment on the political considerations that went into the bail-out of the bank but rather he will focus his investigations on other considerations that led to the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank.
Those questions that are going to be raised by Mr. Justice Estey deserve to be raised and the Canadian taxpayers have the right to know the answers to them. Equally, or I would say even more important, the Canadian taxpayers have a right to demand of their political masters, namely the Government of Canada, in this case the Conservative Government and its front-benchers, political accountability for their actions in this whole process of the bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank.
There are rumours to the effect that the Minister of Finance and his junior Minister, the Minister of State for Finance both personally opposed the bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank. There are other rumours as well, that it was the direct intervention of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) that led to the decision by the Government to bail out the bank. If rumours are correct, and this is why it was rather interesting to hear some of the comments from the Members of Parliament from western Canada, the Prime Minister made his decision not on facts that he had in his hands at that moment but on the basis that he did not want to have the political responsibility to be the Prime Minister of the country at the time when it had its first bank failure in almost 62 years. He wished to make sure that he would not have any

stains on his own being concerning the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank.
For that reason, on the weekend leading to March 25 the Prime Minister and his senior financial advisers, including the two Ministers I mentioned previously, despite the fact that they did not have any idea of the worth of the assets of the Canadian Commercial Bank, decided to bail out the bank. That decision having been made by the Government of Canada, I would like the people here in the galleries and across this country to understand how the political system works. Once that decision was made, representations were made by the Prime Minister and by his Finance Minister to make sure that the Official Opposition in this country would agree to that package bail-out that they had agreed to on that weekend. Frankly, they said, trust us. Here is the trust factor. They said "Trust us when we say that this bail-out package is going to work and, if you raise any serious questions on the floor of the House of Commons in Question Period on Monday, March 25 there is going to be a run on the assets of the Canadian Commercial Bank the like of which you have never seen."
Members of the Government said, "As a responsible Official Opposition, we are asking you to take the words of the Minister of State for Finance, the Minister of Finance and the word of the Prime Minister of this country that the bail-out package that we put together for the Canadian Commercial Bank is going to save that institution."
That was the trust factor that led to our decision on this side of the House to support the bail-out package at that time. Clearly, as has been pointed out today in interventions, the NDP Party wished to have no part of that bail-out. That is fine, they can answer for their Party. I am just indicating to you, Mr. Speaker, that the reason that the Liberal Party acquiesced to the demands for that bail-out were because we trusted the Government and we understood as well, as the Official Opposition, that we had a responsibility to the financial structures of this country and simply do not for frivolous reasons decide not to take the word of a Minister of Finance on such an important issue as the potential failure of a bank in this country. Therefore the trust factor was entered into for the first time.
Since that time we have had reason to doubt why we decided to take the word of these Ministers that I have mentioned but surely it is critical to the political process that when a decision is made, when a Government gives its stamp of approval to a bail-out that the bail-out had better work. As my leader said this morning, if there is going to be a bail-out, make sure to get to the bottom of the boat, get all the water out and keep the boat afloat. What happened in this case was that after the bail-out package was presented on the floor of the House of Commons, it was another three months before the Minister responsible asked for a separate accounting of the assets to occur.
Wrong.

These are the events that have been chronologically put forward by the questions and responses made by the Minister of State for Finance on the floor of the House of Commons. To suggest "wrong", good heavens, Mr. Speaker, if the bail-out was going to work last March 25 the bail-out should never have occurred again in September of this year because the price tags have certainly increased in the intervening six months.
I come back to this trust factor. The Opposition trusted that that bail-out package would work and so did every one of the depositors who had money in those banks. They took the word of the Ministers. Unfortunately the Ministers made a mistake. Clearly something happened from March 25 to September 1 of this year in which the wind-up of the Canadian Commercial Bank was announced by the Minister of State for Finance. In those intervening six months I have no idea about which institutions and which individuals took out moneys and at least saved their deposits, but there were a lot of institutions in this country and a lot of people who took the word of the Government and lost their money.
Therefore, I come back to what is at the heart of the issue. Is it a trust factor? I say it is. What led to the decisions that made for bad management of the Canadian Commercial Bank? Was it the National Energy Program? I scoff at the idea but let's take that suggestion for one moment. It comes as a surprise to me to learn that the Members of Parliament from western Canada want to indicate that it was the National Energy Program that shut down the Canadian Commercial Bank.
Hear, hear!

They do not want us to talk about the mismanagement at the Canadian Commercial Bank. They do not want to talk about the collapse of banks in the State of California, such as the Westland Bank, during the same period of time. There is no National Energy Program in California that I am aware of. They want to quietly go over the fact that the Continental Bank of Illinois collapsed and had to have a bail-out package by its federal Government in the United States in this past 12 months. Was there a National Energy Program in effect south of the border as well? No. I do not have the time so I am not going to digress into what happened as a result of the National Energy Program in some other sectors of the economy in western Canada. The point I am making is that there was bad management at the Canadian Commercial Bank. Those questions will have to be answered by Mr. Justice Estey. I will be very plain about what should be answered on the floor of the House of Commons and that is the political accountability of the two Ministers who guaranteed, in their words, that this bail-out package was going to work. That is why this Bill does nothing, nor does the manoeuvre of getting the problem of the Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank into the hands of Chief Justice Estey take away from the fact that this Government should have political responsibility here.

I want to talk a bit about the essence of the Bill. It is going to cost, as I mentioned earlier, an estimated $875 million of taxpayers' money to undertake the bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. In addition there was the original Bank of Canada's $225 million that was put in. Let us say $1 billion. Let us put that in some perspective. We had a report a year ago that said it would only cost $600 million to clean up International Nickel Company's smelting operations, Noranda Company's smelting operations in Quebec and the Hudson Bay's smelting operations in the Province of Manitoba. These are the smelting operations that have made the major contributions to acid rain in this country. In other words, this bank bail-out is going to cost the Canadian taxpayers more than it would cost to clean up acid rain. That is the perspective that one has to look at. Put another way, and this is the only other thing I am going to have to say about this, it is going to cost every man, woman and child in this country $35 each to bail out this bank.
The Members of Parliament for the Conservative Party sat here, wrapping themselves around the western flag, the Alberta flag, around the fact that these poor depositors need bailouts. Let us take a look at the rationale. I come back to this. A bad decision is a bad decision whether it is made in western Canada, central Canada, Quebec or the Maritimes. That is number one.
Second, before we give approval to the $875-million bailout, we would like to see tabled on the floor of the House of Commons a list of the names of the depositors involved. We have been told by the Minister of State for Finance that she is now wrapping herself in the privacy provisions of the Bank Act. She has said that the Bank Act prevents her from revealing the names of the depositors. We are not dealing with the Bank Act in this legislation. The reason this Bill is before us is because the Bank Act will not allow the Minister to give back moneys to the depositors, and that is why she has come before us with this Bill. Therefore, the Bank Act does not apply in this case and it should not apply in the case of the release of the names of depositors who want their money back.
There is a good, legal case to be made that it is not the Bank Act at issue here nor is it the Bill that is before us. Frankly, what is at issue is part of the Winding-up Act. In my opinion the Winding-up Act allows for a person filing under the Winding-up Act who wishes to have compensation to be forced to sign a release indicating that his name can be made public. It seems fundamental to parliamentary democracy and accountability that when $875 million of taxpayers' money is going out the front door, my constituents should at least know who it is they are using the $875 million to bail out. However, that is not the case. We are told we are not allowed to ask who the depositors are.
I said that this is a very complex subject, and that is quite true. Frankly, most Canadians can better understand the political errors that were made in the "tunagate" affair than they can the failure of the Canadian Commercial Bank. That

does not surprise me because they understand what it means to have a million cans of rancid tuna fish on the supermarket shelves. They can conceptualize what that is all about.
