Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I wish to thank Members of the House for allowing me to proceed with my remarks while seated.
The motion I have before the House today calls for an apology which is half a century overdue. The tragic events that took place on July 1, 1935, in Regina's Old Market Square are an infamous blot on the history of Canada. The events of that day, commonly referred to as the Regina Riot, were, however, at least in hindsight a logical result of the social and economic circumstances of the time.
The social and economic crisis that gripped this and other western countries during the 1930s left few untouched. Thousands of Canadian men and women, blue collar workers, white collar workers and professionals, lost their jobs. Businesses were lost. Farms were lost. Homes were lost. Droves of unemployed workers crossed and recrossed the country in a futile search for non-existent jobs. Soup kitchens, flop-houses and "hobo jungles", where the jobless spent cheerless nights huddled together for companionship, safety and moral support over communal cookpots, sprang up across the country. Farm families, their pitiful possessions loaded in ancient automobiles or on horse-drawn wagons, were a familiar sight on prairie roads in their desperate flight from the drought-ravaged land. The good times were gone. Despair, defeat and depression filled the country.
The Government of the day, which will never be remembered for its generosity and speed of action, was finally forced to respond to the crisis. Relief centres for destitute families were set up across Canada but everywhere it was mean, stingy and humiliating. Even this small measure of cold comfort, however, was not available to everyone. There was no relief for the single, unemployed army of men whom the Government regarded as a potential threat to peace, order and good government. For them, the Government of the day had another solution-the Single Men's Unemployed Relief Work Camps. Here, the men were given meals, a bunk and 20 cents a day spending money, hardly a princely sum even in those days. The men who lived in these camps have described the conditions there as having been very hard.
Official Apology
One man, a founding member of the Relief Camp Workers' Union, provides us with the following description:
The camp rules were British Army rules. The camps were under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence and all the camp superintendents were former World War One army officers, some of whom used to try to put the men through drill... the Government deliberately picked remote spots for the camps. Some were in nice, scenic locations but the camps themselves were terrible. Some were nothing more than tarpaper shacks... The beds varied. Everything from spring cots to wooden bunks. Our clothing consisted of surplus World War One sweaters, pants and boots. They didn't have any of those warm greatcoats left over from World War One. They would have been nice but we all had back jackets and caps. They were new ... The camps, in some cases, were set up around projects. Some of the projects were sensible and had a reasonable purpose but most of the work we did was meaningless, particularly the road (construction) work which had to be redone later on. In a camp of 150 men, there might have been four meaningful jobs. There was no incentive to work ... Every man in the camps was issued a card. When you got thrown out of the camp (for some misdemeanor), the card was stamped on the back. You had one crack at being reinstated if you confessed. When you got blacklisted, they'd transport you out of the camp and dump you miles from anywhere. You were on your own-
Such were the conditions that led to a general strike called by the British Columbia Relief Camp Workers' Union in the late spring of 1935. The camps emptied. One June 3, 1935, a thousand men met at the foot of Gore Avenue on the Vancouver waterfront. They were on their way to Ottawa to put their grievances before the Government of Prime Minister R. B. Bennett. By the time the trekkers reached Regina, their numbers had swelled to 2,000. Unknown to the trekkers, however, Regina, not Ottawa, was the ultimate destination and there the trek was terminated.
At eight o'clock on the evening of July 1, 1935, a mass meeting was in progress on market square in Regina. In the crowd of 2,200 that had gathered to hear a report-back of the trekkers' delegation to Ottawa there were no more than 300 trekkers, many others having gone off to attend a local ball game. On the platform sat representatives of the local city council, the citizens' committee and the trekkers' committee. Jerry Winters, a member of the trekkers' committee, was in the process of making an appeal when his words were cut short by the sharp blast of a police whistle. Suddenly, mounted members of the RCMP poured from the huge vans that had pulled up on three sides of the square. Armed with batons, they charged into the crowd and disrupted the meeting which, until that moment, had been entirely peaceful and orderly. Onlookers were clubbed to the ground, making them instant "recruits" to the trekkers' cause. Joined by Regina citizens and armed only with makeshift clubs, the trekkers fought back against police officers armed with guns. The shooting and fighting continued until midnight. When the smoke cleared, one police officer lay dead, 21 other people were taken to hospital for treatment of injuries and 120 citizens and trekkers were arrested.
Police reports and newspaper accounts of the day have left a misleading impression of the circumstances surrounding the riot, laying blame for the riot on the heads of the trekkers. Much of what was written then and unfortunately believed to this day is nothing more than a "masterpiece of lies" as one trekker has described it. I repeat that the assembly was

October 7, 1985
Official Apology
peaceful and only broken up on orders from the Government in Ottawa.
The facts of the case are that the riot was planned and provoked, not by the trekkers, but by the police on direct orders of the federal Government which, in so doing, illegally usurped the authority of the provincial Government which was in the process of negotiating a settlement with the trekkers. Such action, Mr. Speaker, not only warrants an apolicy but begs forgiveness.
The motion I have placed before the House might merely be regarded as a footnote to history were it not for the fact that history has a tendency to repeat itself. The sad fact of the matter is that the History I have just outlined is in many ways and many places across this country repeating itself today. Many of the problems for which the trekkers sought solutions in the 1930s have returned in spades in the 1980s. Once again we have massive unemployment. Once again we are faced with widespread business failures, farm foreclosures, personal bankruptcies and food banks.
The parallels which can be drawn between 1935 and 1985 are truly staggering. Even nature has co-operated by providing prairie farmers with a return engagement of the drought and grasshopper epidemic which plagued their parents and grandparents 50 years ago. Once obvious parallel for which nature cannot be given credit, however, is the return engagement of a Conservative Government in Ottawa with identical attitudes in an identical situation. A little more than 50 years ago Conservative R. B. Bennett promised to "end unemployment or perish in the attempt". Last year the present Progressive Conservative Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised "jobs, jobs, jobs". Fifty years ago the Conservative Prime Minister, R. B. Bennett, espoused "imperial preference" as the key to economic recovery. Today the Progressive Conservative Prime Minister espouses the private sector and free trade with the United States as the key to economic recovery.
One and a half million jobless Canadians, men and women, young and not-so-young, cannot be written off. As much as the Government opposite might wish, they will not disappear or go away for the simple reason that they have nowhere to go except, perhaps, to fall further down into a sea of entirely understandable despair and disillusionment on their part.
What does 1.5 million unemployed Canadians really mean? To economists and statisticians it means a nice round figure that can be played with and juggled about on paper with relative ease. To the Government opposite it probably means a pain in the neck that refuses to go away. To the country as a whole, however, it means a shameful waste of precious human resources. To the 1.5 million Canadian men and women who find themselves without work and with little hope of finding work, it means personal disaster. To the unemployed auto worker with a family to support and a mortgage to be paid it means the probable loss of a home. To the unemployed professional-and their numbers are growing every day-it means a greatly reduced standard of living all too often
culminating in a one-way ticket to poverty. To the unemployed single mother it frequently means welfare and a day-to-day struggle just to keep herself and her children fed, never mind adequately clothed. To the unemployed young person just graduated from high school, technical school, or university, it means a wasted effort and a future without hope. That is what unemployment really means, Mr. Speaker.
What does the Government opposite propose to do about this most grave situation? Leave it to the private sector, that is where the jobs will be created we are told. We are told that but we do not believe it and neither do the 1.5 million unemployed Canadians whose lives are being wasted by the do-nothing attitude of a pass-the-buck Government.
Massive unemployment and its attendant social problems, contrary to what the Government opposite might wish to believe, is not the result of an act of God, Mr. Speaker. It is a man-made problem and it demands a man-made Government-led solution. Unfortunately, the solution to such massive unemployment as we are faced with today will never be found by leaving it to the private sector and various applications of the tried-but-not-true trickle down economic theory. We need solid, sensible action by Government on unemployment and we need it now.
Canada is not a poor nation despite the obsessive pleas of the Government opposite regarding our deficit. Canada is a rich nation in both natural and human resources. We have vast natural resources that lie waiting to be developed and a highly educated, highly skilled workforce waiting to be allowed to develop those resources. We are not only a rich nation, we are a young nation, and much remains to be done. Much remains to be done in agriculture, in forestry, in industry, in education, in health care, in communications, and in technology. We have hundreds of projects which lie crying to be undertaken. We have hundreds of thousands of jobs that lie crying to be created and hundreds of thousands of unemployed Canadians waiting to fill those jobs. We cannot leave that to the private sector alone, Mr. Speaker. It is the responsibility of the Government to ensure that those projects are undertaken and those jobs created.
We cannot wait for a solution to unemployment to fall from the sky. That is what the Government did 50 years ago when the solution to the unemployment problem of that ear finally arrived in the form of a world war. Such a solution in this day and age would mean the end of civilization. I do not mean to suggest for a second that the Government opposite would ever consider such a solution to our present unemployment problem. What 1 do mean to suggest, Mr. Speaker, is that the Government should take a lesson from the past and undertake sensible and constructive projects that will put people back to work and this country on the road to economic recovery and prosperity.
Fifty years ago a handful of tired, hungry, destitute trekkers tried to do something about unemployment and were beaten and insulted by a callous and uncaring Conservative Government. The survivors of that valiant group of men deserve an apology from this Government for the actions of the Govern-
October 7, 1985

ment of that day. This is not a new idea, Mr. Speaker. I remind the House that on June 29, 1984, the former Leader of the Opposition and present Prime Minister asked the Government of the day to apologize to the Japanese Canadians. He said:
I am asking him if he will rise to the occasion and convey, on behalf of the Government of Canada, a genuine apology to Canadian citizens who were so badly done by.
1 use the same words of the then Leader of the Opposition to appeal to him and to his Government to apologize to those Canadians who were so badly done by that previous Conservative Government.
There is much more that can be done, that must be done for the mean and women who today face the same problems experienced by the trekkers half a century ago. I hope the House will unanimously and whole-heartedly accept the motion that I have placed before it. I understand as well, Mr. Speaker, that after the Prime Minister met with the trekkers earlier this year he promised to give serious consideration to their request for an official apology and said that he would take this matter to Cabinet. I hope that when we hear from the spokesperson of the Government that he or she will indicate the Government's support for the resolution that I have placed before the House today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) on making his speech in difficult physical circumstances. I realize he felt it was his duty to be here in the House today, and I think that is admirable, although I do not agree with the text of his motion.
Mr. Speaker, from the text it is clear that what is being asked is an unequivocal apology. I would have expected the Hon. Member to concentrate more on showering abuse on a Government that refuses to side with the workers, since today, there is a tendency to say that the same situation may be repeated.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to take part in the debate, because I have been active in the labour movement, both as a union member and member of an association. I also worked for twelve years on the management side as a negotiator in collective bargaining sessions at the local and provincial levels. I am also pleased because the motion before the House today, which of course refers to the past, to events that occurred 50 years ago, also goes back to a time in history which I find it interesting to recall, as a former history teacher.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I think the Government will conclude by saying, I do not think, I am sure that the best way to build the future is to look to the past, to analyze events, and instead of constantly apologizing for what happened in the past, to be prepared to change things for the better.
Official Apology
Mr. Speaker, 50 years ago, conditions were terrible. It was in the beginning of the thirties, in fact during 1930-40 eight or nine years before the war, the Great Depression, when economic conditions were poor, and the Government at the time did not have the kind of economic leverage that we have today, and people did the best they could according to the time-honoured method of trial and error.
I remember when I was younger, at Sainte-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere, when my grandfather was terribly insulted when the first Old Age Security pensions came through, because old people had to declare their income. It was not an ideal situation, but instead of spending our time apologizing to these people because we forced them to make these declarations, what did we do? We established a different and necessarily better system.
That is past experience. The same thing goes for family allowances and a great many social measures which did not exist in those days but which we enjoy today. Mr. Speaker, I do not have to apologize for my father's or my grandfather's actions because had my grandfather chosen a different field of activity I might be a little bit richer today. I do not have to apologize for that.
History does teach us that it ought to be used to understand rather than to accuse, and I rely on historians to relate what went on in Government. We will analyze the situation and attempt to benefit from all those trying experiences so as to leave something better for our children.
So with respect to the past, Mr. Speaker, we must always keep the historical context in mind, never forget that the passage of time clears up past incidents which must be viewed in their proper perspective. I would suggest that my colleague is getting carried away when he claims that history is repeating itself right now.
All we need do is examine some figures or data. For the past five or six months, Mr. Speaker, I have been working on the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program-ILAP for short. Mistakes were made and corrected, and again last week benefits paid by the employer and deposited in a trust account were deducted from benefits available under ILAP. A change had been made on October 16, not through a ministerial order, but by amending the regulations, and then was implemented- Your Honour knows how fast we are-on April 25. As soon as we realized that a mistake had been made, instead of apologizing for that mistake, we tried to remedy the situation, which has been done as of last week.
Was it a mistake? When the Department of Justice analyzed the last ILAP proposals, did it make a mistake? I cannot answer in term of mistake, but what I can say, though, is that we have taken into account the working men and women who had based their decisions to retire early on their expectation as to their income: they would get their unemploy-

October 7, 1985
Official Apology
ment insurance benefits, as well as their early retirement benefits and a Government program. Now, their Government program was being taken away from them.
Instead of apologizing to them, Mr. Speaker, what we did out of respect for them was to change the regulations. That was important to understand the historical background. There is not a Government, not a politician, not a single member on either side of the House, who enjoyed certain events that happened in the province of Quebec. I am referring to the strike of asbestos-industry workers which was a turning point in the history of union development in Quebec and contributed more to the establishment of a labour code in that province than hours after hours of interminable discussions in an assembly.
When the Quebec government or the Iron Ore decided to close its operation in Schefferville, I can say that the negotiations that took place at this occasion has helped us achieve some progress, and I was able to realize that when the Quebec Government decided to close the town of Gagnon located North of Sept-Iles. If experiences such as those of Schefferville have helped us in the case of the town of Gagnon, the Gagnon experience will in turn help us settle other problems. The idea is not to apologize but to work harder for a better future.
My hon. colleague says that he is afraid that the same thing will happen and that the situation might come up once again. I do not think it can, Mr. Speaker.
You just have to look at some of the figures. In fact, let us take the first figure, which is the Gross National Product. It has increased annually by 4.1 per cent. This increase in the GNP is very important in assessing the situation, and I do not think that the same conditions existed in the 30's.
There is another interesting figure, Mr. Speaker. We have 284,000 less unemployed now as 284,000 jobs have been created since last year. Unemployment has fallen from 11.6 per cent in September 1984 to 10.3 per cent in August 1985. Youth unemployment has also fallen from 18.3 per cent to 15.9 per cent. This is still high, but the situation is under control and the rate is going down. Another figure which is often forgotten and which has a direct effect on all working men and women concerns the interest rates. Current interest rates in Canada are lower than they have been in the past seven or eight years.
It is not only the Members of Parliament who pay lower interest rates, but ordinary workers. These are ordinary people and consumers. For instance, the amount spent on car purchases or current expenses have increased by 25 per cent since last year. This also has an impact. As a Government, we should not be content with spending our time making excuses for the past. Instead, we should build better conditions for the future, conditions without uncertainty, and try to control them as much as possible. The interest rates are a very important factor for consumers, in building a house, in obtaining individual loans or in getting commercial loans. Mr. Speaker,
the confidence of investors is important for the future of the Quebec economy.
According to a Conference Board survey, 53 per cent of owners want to make investments in the coming year, while 8 per cent do not want to do so and the remainder are undecided. What does this show, Mr. Speaker? It shows that people are confident in the future and are willing to gamble on it. Moreover, Statistics Canada says that capital expenditures have increased by 12 per cent in 1985. All these facts show that the conditions have changed.
Mr. Speaker, consumer expenditures have increased by 12 per cent. The increase has been 23 per cent in automotive purchases alone, as I mentioned earlier. Here is a clue, a sign as people say, that conditions are not as they were in 1930. Times are bad, but not as bad as in 1930. The number of building permits has increased by 19 per cent. In 1930, I doubt the increase was as high. The consumer price index has never been that stable since 1971, and statistics are self eloquent: 4 per cent. We have the most stable consumer price index since 1971. The conditions are not the same. This is the best token of consideration that can be given workers, giving them those conditions rather than having to apologize. Bankruptcies have been fewer. Economic activity is on the upswing. All that, Mr. Speaker, to say that the best token of consideration that can be give to a worker, instead of apologizing, is not to prevent a recurrence of those conditions, and to work arduously, in cooperation.
We may disagree-the Opposition Party, the New Democratic Party-we may disagree as to the means, but the facts are there and must be taken into consideration.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, interest rates for eight years-we are just out of last year's election, and that matter of interest rates has been a sensitive issue for the Official Opposition. But rates are now the lowest in eight years. Those are facts!
They can argue. They can say this is not the right way of doing it. They may say it is our fault, it is not our fault! But the facts are there, Mr. Speaker.
As I said, the best way to honour a worker is to provide him with better economic conditions. The best way to correct a mistake, in my experience as a personnal manager, was not to send letters of apologies to everyone, it was to try and not to repeat the same error twice, and when I did so you may be sure that they confronted me with it. They said: "Besides memory, I think you also lack judgment." This is the way to show people consideration, Mr. Speaker.
For all those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I think we are building something sound, and one of the efficient tools we have now set up is the new employment strategy the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) announced in this House. This is an employment strategy that is based first on flexibility, and second on agreement with the Provinces.
October 7, 1985

There are six possible ways in which this may be developed, and for the first time, Mr. Speaker, we have a program that is not readymade in Ottawa and undiversified for the whole country, because previously, whether you came from Nova Scotia or British Columbia, your program was the same. Now we have divided it along regions, and there will be six possible avenues. A region may chose this option or this strategy, rather than another one.
Mr. Speaker, this is not all. We have even thought that in a given Province, in the district of Regina, Hamilton or Valley-field, according to circumstances, there were employment development trails that could be more interesting. This is something that we did! First we must show flexibility and then try to reach an agreement or seek a consensus. All manpower centres will have working committees which will call upon working men and women.
Mr. Speaker, a case in point is the new Jobs Strategy, its guiding principles and its purposes, all geared to basic training. All employment development programs are based on training, and that is what we call building for the future. We want to make sure that tomorrow will be more than a slightly indexed yesterday! That is what the Government has been working on for a year, Mr. Speaker, and the results are promising. Some 284,000 jobs have been created and there will be more now that the new strategy has been set in motion.
That is an important consideration, Mr. Speaker, for we know we have to attract the private sector. Not only do we attract private sector interests, but we get them involved and tell them: We need you, we will support you and you will create new jobs.
All that has been set in motion, Mr. Speaker, but I do not think past conditions reflect the current situation. Most important, we must not fall asleep or gaze at our navels. A lot remains to be done because a 15.9 per cent unemployment rate among youths is still much too high even though we made some progress since it once stood at 18.3 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, the best homage we can pay working men and women or the union movement which did much for the economic expansion of our country is to encourage them to build a different future and call upon every available resource to make sure that we will indeed have a more promising future and not repeat past mistakes.
Mr. Speaker, again I say that we respect working men and women as well as unions and management. A good Government relies upon its people, Mr. Speaker, and I suggest that our Government has made a commendable effort in that direction.

Mr. Speaker, we have just heard, according to the Hon. Member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Hudon), that even considering what was said
Official Apology
to workers and the unemployed 50 years ago, we should not apologize to them because we must look to the future.
Mr. Speaker, if we consider the case made by Japanese Canadians, and if we look at other situations and even the Riel case which was examined in the House since I became a Member of Parliament, it is quite obvious that if we want to understand the future, if we want to act responsibly as a Government, and in our dealings with young people or the unemployed, everyone ought to know what happened under a Conservative Government 50 years ago. And we, both as Members and as the Government, should apologize to the unemployed workers who were forced to take to the streets to seek their own rights which they should have been given by the Prime Minister at the time, who abdicated his responsibilities in this respect.
I think it would be useful for all students of Canadian history, not just for us who are considering the problem in Parliament today in a rather abstract context, if we could look at the situation as it was in 1935. We know very well, for instance, that it was a terrible time for all unemployed in all the provinces. And I quote:

Beyond the evidence of the human condition there are the statistics drawn here from the report of the Royal Commission on Dominion Provincial Relations on an index of 100 for July, 1929 on unemployment. In 1929 there were 107,000 unemployed workers across Canada. By 1933 there were 646,000. Per capita incomes across the country had fallen dramatically and at an appalling rate. We see, between 1929 and 1933, that the income in the Province of Saskatchewan alone fell by 72 per cent. The per capital income in Alberta fell by 61 per cent. In the Province of Ontario it fell by 44 per cent and in P.E.I. 45 per cent. In British Columbia it fell by 47 per cent; in New Brunswick by 39 per cent and in Nova Scotia by 36 per cent.
What was the federal Government's response at that time? Was it in fact to assist in programs which would facilitate municipalities and provinces to develop work programs? No. It took the same attitude as this Government is taking. That is it wants a hands-off approach. It does not want to be involved in the creation of jobs because somehow Conservative Governments see something distasteful in direct Government job-creation. In fact, the Bennett solution at that time was to send the workers off to work camps where they lived in intolerable circumstances and in fact were not ever able to have the dignity of a democratic election in those particular camps.
We know the situation and I would agree the support systems that have been built over the past 20 years here, no thanks to the Conservative Government, have in fact led to a situation where in the recession that we suffered over the last couple of years the workers were not as hard hit as they were in the Great Depression. For those of us who did not live in that time, I think it behooves all of us to look at history, to consider the situation as cited in the report of the Royal Commission. Canada had never again experienced an unemployment problem of such magnitude. During previous periods

October 7, 1985
Official Apology
of economic depression the problems of unemployment and destitution had usually found their solution in self-sufficiency; self-sufficiency of the household; solidarity of the family; the establishment of new homes on the agricultural frontier and the increase of emigration to the United States. By the 1930s such opportunities had all but disappeared.
We know that the workers were in a desperate situation. In fact it was spoken in the Elouse of Commons in the words of J. S. Woodsworth, and I think this question applies today in 1985 when we are hearing about the unemployment figures of 15 per cent and 16 per cent among young people, and this is the quote:
-I do suggest that you cannot expect young men in the prime of life-
Of course, in those days they did not talk about young women, but it continues:
-young men in the prime of life to go into these camps to get a bare living month after month, and some of them, year after year, without their losing hope. I think of the moral influences which prevail in such places. Young men who under normal circumstances would have a certain amount of social life and would look forward to marrying and rearing their own families are now deprived of all the amenities of home life and are simply kept in these camps for an indefinite future. Really I wonder that there are not more criminal acts in this country than there have been in the immediate past.
The book goes on:
A growing conviction seems to have entered the minds of most of the men that they are a forgotten group. The isolation of many of the camps renders it impossible for men to keep in touch personally with former employment or with new work opening up. It is true that the Provincial Labour Bureau does seek to bring men in camps to the attention of employers-yet the employment of the men from the Relief Camps is so rare that a fixed idea prevails among the men that they are deemed unsuitable for employment, and are shunned by those seeking workmen.
We can see the sense of desperation that had arisen at that time. I am sure the Government of this day, being of a Progressive Conservative stripe, can argue that we should look to the future and not dwell on the past. However, I would suggest that if we look to another Conservative government, we would see the difficulties that are currently being experienced in the great country of Great Britain. There has been so much hopelessness and despair felt by young people in Britain that it has led them to violence and that is the kind of hopelessness and despair that we in Parliament should address before we see the same kind of situation arising here in Canada.
Hon. Members of the Government side can say that apologies or excuses have no place in a plan for employment for our young people. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Hudon) has spoken of the Government programs. We know that the programs that have been instituted by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) are too little too late.
We know that the current regional program is in a shambles because employers are not taking up the 25 per cent subsidy that was offered by the Government on make-work programs in the private sector. We know that there are very serious problems that have manifested themselves in Government
Departments across this country because instead of adopting a program that had already been put in place by the Liberal Government, the First Chance Program, the Minister of Employment and Immigration took it upon herself to wash her hands of any Liberal initiative and to leave young people waiting for weeks, months and in some cases years for their first chance to get out into the workforce.
For those of us in the House who are really concerned not only about the unemployment of our young but about the unemployment of older people, I think that the record of the Government with respect to older workers is as shameful as was the record of the Bennett Government with respect to those who were driven into work camps. I cite the insidious provisions that have been instituted by the Minister of Employment and Immigration to gouge older workers, to cut their severance benefits and to make them use up their holiday pay by insisting that as of next January, they must exhaust all pension benefits before they can collect unemployment insurance. We heard an Hon. Member say today how wonderful it was that they had discovered a discrepancy between the amount of money that employers paid in ILAP areas paid into unemployment insurance and the amount paid by those in other areas.
As soon as the discrepancy in the employer program was discovered, the Government acted quickly. It moved in to make sure that employers were not paying too much into the program. In fact, in 1985, older workers who are in their fifties and sixties many of whom have no real chance for future employment, the same as in 1935, have to spend every last penny of their pension benefits, severance benefits and holiday pay before they can collect one dime from the Government. That is the kind of compassion and humanity that we see coming from the Conservative Government of 1985.
I would suggest that when speaking of a lost generation, the lost generation is not only the youth but also those older men and women who have been replaced through technological change, the euphemism for being replaced by machines and becoming redundant. These people have been hit by Government indecision and waffling on issues such as the shoe quotas. In my riding, there are literally hundreds of jobs that are currently being threatened by the Government's failure to act. In a sense, these men and women are facing the same situation as those men and women in the work camps faced some 50 years ago.
In my riding, the unemployment rate is at over 10 per cent across the board and not only among young people. Older workers, many of whom may not have a great command of the English language, knock on doors. They may have an old back injury or they may be 55 years of age and greying. They may not have the kind of marketable skills that would put them back into the market-place. They are being turned away. Those people are members of a lost generation and a generation the Government has a responsibility to address through specific Government-initiated job-creation programs.
It is folly for the Minister of Employment and Immigration to say that the private sector will help these people out. We
October 7, 1985

saw what the private sector had to say to the Minister when she commented on the corporate behaviour of INCO in the riding of Sudbury. We saw what kind of corporate response came from that company when it came to developing an agreement with the union in that particular industry. It seems to me that in this area, we have a responsibility to lead, not to follow. We also have a responsibility to ensure that Government programs are not whittled away while we wait for private-sector response to a 25 per cent subsidy in the job market.
It is my understanding that the 25 per cent subsidy program is not working and that it is in shambles across the country, notwithstanding the fact that it was with great brouhaha and fanfare that the Minister announced the program at the beginning of September. More than a month later, many of those programs are not yet operational. They are still waiting to be launched because the Minister has not even passed along the information to regional Departments regarding what will be offered and what is necessary.
That being said, I think it is clear that one way of clearing the record and beginning the new trek is to say to those Depression workers and their families, just as we said to the families of those Japanese Canadians who were wrongly interned, that we were wrong and made a mistake. We should say that we are sorry. While it may not mean much in terms of individual compensation for the agony suffered by those people who lived through the Depression, it would certainly be a first step on the road to clearing the record. There is a saying with which I am sure Members of the House are familiar and that is that "Tory times are tough times". Dating back to the days of the Great Depression and the days of the Bennett Government, there is a sense that when times were tough, instead of reaching out to help workers, the Government of the day reached out to line the pockets of the rich, wealthy, powerful and famous.
It seems to me that we saw a manifestation of this same sense in the first Conservative Budget of this administration. In that Budget, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said to the Canadian people that they would cut back on baby bonuses, reduce increases in family allowances and at the same time offer a $500,000 capital gains tax write-off to that top 4 per cent of the population that is in a position to take advantage of it.
What about the farmers?

We are not talking about the farmers. Of course Members will talk about the farmers. The farmers will only benefit when they sell out. Most of the farmers I know want to hang on to their land. That Budget offered nothing for those farmers. At the same time, there is an underlying Conservative philosophy that, "Them that has, gets, and them that hasn't gets put down even further". That is why we are concerned and fearful and rightfully dismayed when reading about the kinds of initiatives that this Government has undertaken with respect to older workers.

Can't hear you.
Official Apology

The Hon. Member may not be able to hear me but the people of Canada are getting the message that this Government was elected on a platform of broken promises. The Prime Minister cannot be trusted to believe that universality is a sacred trust. As soon as the Minister of Employment and Immigration was given the chance, she moved in to cut away on workers' pensions, workers' severance benefits and workers' holiday pay. Yes, even as we speak in the House of Commons, those employees of this place who did not have their pension benefits deducted are now being penalized by monthly deductions from their pay cheques for a mistake which was made by the Government and for which they had no responsibility. I am speaking of House of Commons employees who earn somewhere in the neighbourhood of $12,000 to $15,000 a year. They are not living in the lap of luxury. However, as soon as the Government discovered its mistake it moved in quickly to institute automatic salary deductions from those employees in the same way as it is suggesting to workers who have been laid off at companies such as Consolidated Bathurst in Hamilton that their pension funds, holiday pay and severance benefits should be taken into account before they collect one cent of unemployment insurance. Consolidated Bathurst is a company which shut its doors no more to open. Employees with 30 years of service have been let go. The average length of service at the company was about 24 to 25 years. I am speaking of people who invested their lives, hopes and dreams in a company which has closed its doors. If this particular piece of legislation had been in place at that time, those employees would have been required to liquidate every last penny of their pension funds, as well as their holiday pay and their severance benefits, before they could collect one cent of unemployment insurance.
The people of Canada recognize that this Government initiative is wrong. They further recognize that there comes a point in the life of any man or woman when the ordinary channels of law do not succeed. We have seen that in the "On To Ottawa" trek. They called the politicians. The Prime Minister met them with deaf ears. They contacted their provincial officials and, in fact, were given no satisfaction.
I would like to quote for the record a comment made by one of the trekkers when he spoke directly with the Prime Minister of Canada at that time. He said:
-I was satisfied that Mr. Bennett was not there for he had not been prepared to deal with us sympathetically or to discuss in detail any of our demands. So that I did not think it was necessary for me to accept any more of his bullying and brow-beating and when he told me I was a thief, then I told him he was a liar... He said, "You have just come out of the penitentiary at Westminster." Objection was taken to this encounter by Mr. Cosgrove.
Mr. Speaker, do you know what those men were seeking in terms of justice for Canadian workers? They had a list of demands which were considered communist by the Prime Minister of the day. The list of demands included something as simple as work wages being instituted at a minimum of 50 cents per hour for unskilled workers and trade union rates for skilled work being instituted on the basis of a six-hour day,

October 7, 1985
Official Apology
five-day week, with a minimum of 20 work days a month. They wanted to work, but they wanted to do it for a living wage. Can Members of the House imagine how revolutionary it was for these people to ask that all workers in relief camps be covered by the Compensation Act? They asked that adequate first aid supplies be carried on the job at all times. Those were some of the requests which the Government found so heinous that it would not allow them to even come to Ottawa. They were stopped in Saskatchewan. The borders were closed, as were the rails. These people were prevented from coming to Ottawa to express their democratic God-given rights for better conditions in the work camps. They also asked that the system of blacklisting with respect to national defence and all military control in which men are cut off from all means of livelihood be abolished. They asked for a discontinuance of blacklisting, Mr. Speaker. That was a simple request. They also asked that democratically elected committees be recognized in every camp.
I do not think these requests by the trekkers were heinous enough to have resulted in the type of brutal application of government force which we saw in 1935. I further feel as a Canadian it is important for this Government today, in 1985, if it is truly sincere about beginning to gain back the confidence of young working people, young unemployed people, older working people and older unemployed people to realize that the time has come for it to endorse an all-Party resolution which calls for an apology to redress an event which occurred 50 years ago and which is indicative of the type of Conservative mentality which has led all Canadians to realize that Tory times are tough times.
The Government has its chance today. Private Members have their chance today. They can stand up and vote in favour of a democratically elected institution and vote for democracy. They can stand up and make to these people a general, all-encompassing public apology. I suggest that that act of good faith and of goodwill on the part of the Government would begin to restore the credibility which this Government has lost in insisting upon measures which are anti-worker, anti-family, anti-labour and anti-union with respect to the type of measures we have seen outlined in our discussions today.
Work must be done or the Government's word cannot be believed. Now is the chance for the Government to win back some of the credibility it has frittered away since September 4.

Mr. Speaker, we have just discovered that if you sit while you speak you get a bum speech. I have certainly noticed that the speeches we have heard fit that category absolutely. We have heard about an issue which took place some 50 years ago. Some of the debate has been twisted in order to put it in a perspective relevant to today. All this under the guise of a Private Member's Bill to advocate socialism! In all of the singsong which the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) has put forward with respect to the riot of 1935 he spoke about one person having been killed. He ought to have mentioned that the person who was killed was a police officer.

These are the people who, in their mentality, would like to take the time of the House of Commons to apologize. They would apologize for the Acadians, for small pox given to the Indians, for the tooth decay of the Inuit, for the Chinese Canadians who built the railway and for the FLQ crisis. They would have us apologize to Oregon and Washington because the British Empire did not act fast enough to make them part of Canadian territory. Members opposite wish to rewrite history. They have read up on Engels and they know about Joseph Stalin. They know about how those two rewrote history. They say: "That is for me. Let us rewrite the stuff."
Today, we are talking about a crisis which was world-wide 50 years ago. It was not just a Canadian crisis. It was something which was taking place in the United States, north and west Europe, the Soviet Union and throughout the British Empire. A world-wide Depression was taking place. The Depression occurred because at that period of time in history countries were building protectionist walls around each other. They were building walls so that the economies could not expand. All around the world in 1935, before the Depression, country after country was saying: "It is me. It is mine."
We stand here today after having come through the last few years which were solely concerned with protectionism. Today, the Government says: "Let's open up. Let's use efficiency and initiative so that we can get our products on the world markets. Let's open up trade initiatives." Yet, what is the response of Liberals and New Democrats to that forward piece of thinking? They say: "Do not talk with the United States. Let's close our borders." These are the very people who came here today to apologize for 1935. They are asking to do the same thing as that which took place in 1935. They want us to close up the borders and not talk to the Americans about expanded trade. They are saying that they want to have it all here in Canada without a world market. subtopic: CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-SERVICE AT BLUE WATER BRIDGE INTERNATIONAL CROSSING
CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-SERVICE AT BLUE WATER BRIDGE INTERNATIONAL CROSSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to talk about a particular and very serious problem in my area. Personnel of the Blue Water Bridge Authority at Sarnia have compiled statistics for me which detail the extent of the traffic back-up on the bridge over the last number of months. These statistics were recorded at 15 minute intervals for four months, from April 29 to August 31, 1985. What these statistics reveal to me is that there is a very serious problem which must be addressed as soon as possible.
Until the end of June there were six custom lanes available for use by customs officers at the Blue Water bridge. In July of this year, the seventh lane was constructed. However, due to a shortage of customs personnel and staff-and we are again threatened with further cut-backs-only half of the available seven lanes were staffed most of this summer with customs officers. Because of this, 44 per cent of the lanes were closed but traffic flows, if anything, continued to increase daily. As a matter of fact, car traffic is up 5 per cent and truck traffic is up a fantastic 20 per cent over 1984.
While this may not seem so terrible because 56 per cent of the lanes were open, in reality this causes back-ups and/or a waiting period of anywhere from 10 minutes to an astronomical five hours, which makes the severity of the situation very apparent and lends to it a note of urgency for action.
On certain occasions during peak periods there is a back-up of vehicles waiting a horrendous two hours just to get over the bridge. This results in cars, buses, transport trucks, in fact all motor vehicles being backed up the full length of the Blue Water bridge and onto the 1-94 freeway which approaches the bridge on the Michigan, United States, side.
I would like to cite a few examples. On August 15 at 11.30 a.m. the cars and trucks were backed up 7,000 feet on the bridge. At 1.30 p.m. vehicles were still backed up 3,500 feet, which resulted in a two-hour clearance time. On May 24 five lanes were open at 5.50 p.m. and the cars and trucks were backed up for 2,500 feet. At 6.15 p.m., with the same number of lanes open, the back-up was approximately 5,500 feet for a four hour and thirty-five minute time to clear.
Adjournment Debate
1 know my colleague, the Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz), has similar problems with the bridge in his constituency. I think I can speak on behalf of the tourists who come to Sarnia-Lambton by saying that when faced with such a lengthy delay it would be very easy to throw in the towel and turn around and go home.
It seems ludicrous to me that we now have a Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. Murta) who is placing this year, for the first time, greater emphasis on the beneficial effects of a productive tourist industry, and yet we make it so very difficult for these tourists to come into our country to spend their dollars and boost our economy. I feel that if we do not begin to remove the causes of this problem, we will not have to worry about the tourism industry because we will be lacking the one essential ingredient-tourists.
On the July 4 weekend traffic was backed up on the Blue Water bridge 3,500 feet and there was a five hour clearance time on the bridge on that particular day. Such delays add much frustration to the tourists and does much to discourage Americans and Canadian tourists from western Canada who come to our area via that route, from visiting my area and the rest of Ontario and Canada through this very important port.
Considering that tourism is an $18 billion a year industry and employs more than 600,000 Canadians directly and thousands more indirectly, I believe this is very good reason to look at the problem seriously and make every effort to find a solution. The Government must stop cutting off the right hand with the left hand, as in this case.
I would like to address the problem we are facing with trucks attempting to clear customs. While there are two specific Customs lanes available for clearance, on all problem occasions only one booth was open, again through the shortage and/or deployment of customs personnel. Particular trucks were faced with delays of anywhere from 10 minutes to one hour and fifteen minutes to get through those lanes. Delays are occurring in all instances, even when trucks wish to leave our country. They are probably trucking those very important Canadian exports into the United States.
The outbound booth for traffic is supposed to be manned 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Yet, it has been noted that this booth was closed for 157 hours during this review period. This forces the driver to park his truck and cross three busy lanes of westbound traffic in order to have the appropriate documentation arranged in order to allow him to leave. Must we wait until a serious traffic accident occurs before we act to correct this matter? We should not stand by while our exports are being held up.
Also, during the review period customs employed an extra 12 students. I am concerned about how these students were deployed and whether there was the flexibility to deploy them in the proper manner so that they would be most effective. I suspect that this did not happen.
It is imperative that we find a way to get people across the bridge and through customs more expeditiously. Our inability
7426

October 7, 1985
Adjournment Debate
to do this affects the attitudes of our visitors. I believe that word of mouth is one way to either completely enhance or suffocate our tourist industry. It also effects the commerce and thus the well-being and standard of living of the community and the country, as well as affecting the ability of our customs officers, as first-line officers, to do their job properly. If we must, I suggest that we find a means to make the existing quota of person years for customs officers work more efficiently and effectively for us.
I believe that the solution is simple. We need to consider having more rather than less personnel at those first-line positions, as well as flexibility for deployment of those first-line officers. This becomes even more crucial when we consider that the 1-69 Freeway through the State of Michigan, which will be completed soon, will bring even more traffic through and across the Blue Water bridge.
There is a positive working relationship between the Blue Water Bridge Authority and the customs management. Over $70 million in duties was realized at that bridge last year. It is a very important port.
It would seem that the domino effect is very strong in this particular case. Actions of the customs officers affect the tourism industry and the commerce of the area and the increased traffic flows with the decreasing number of staff manning the booths do little to relieve the problem.
I urge the Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) to act on this matter swiftly. I offer my assistance to them in any way which may help correct this problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue and Canada Post):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-SERVICE AT BLUE WATER BRIDGE INTERNATIONAL CROSSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for raising this issue and offering to co-operate with us. Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that the level of services offered by Customs at Sarnia's Blue Water Bridge in Ontario is presently under on-going monitoring. Monitoring has revealed that in certain cases many factors may have contributed to delays and traffic tie-ups.
Improvements to the main local highways-the link between Interstate 69 in the United States and Highways 402 and 401 between Sarnia and London, among others-have contributed to higher traffic density. Roughly 6 per cent more passenger cars and 20 per cent more trucks have used the Blue Water Bridge. In addition, traffic figures were 54 per cent higher than in winter.
Customs noted four incidents which led to abnormally long delays this past summer. Delays resulted from problems related to work hour schedules and unexpected traffic density. Customs officials agree that customs clearing has to be made easier, but as you know, Mr. Speaker, they are responsible for making sure that our laws are applied and respected.
The Department of National Revenue, Customs and Excise, constantly monitors traffic trends at the Blue Water Bridge to
establish peak hours and make sure that enough employees are on duty, as recommended by my colleague. In addition, better use of part time and seasonal employees during summer peak periods will contribute to increase regular staff so that the level of services will be adequate and generally acceptable.
Now that students hired for the summer are gone, more part time employees will be on duty in October 1985. Those part time employees are added to the regular staff, something we found necessary as a result of last summer's monitoring.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Minister of Customs and Excise has told the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) and myself that there is no plan to reduce the number of inspectors at the Blue Water Bridge. There are now 89 year-persons at that location, including 50 for border traffic operations.

I did not hear about 1,500 jobs from me or from anyone else who has responsibility for the matter. In fact, that was a newspaper report and of course is not the figure that anyone else is using.

And that was followed by "

Hear, hear!"
Mr. Speaker, I was not talking through my hat 20 minutes later, when I told the Minister: You talked to us about 1,500 jobs. He said as much himself. So perhaps the Minister would like to apologize because he implied to me or at least the House that I was spreading false rumours, and I do not like
October 7, 1985

that sort of thing. He may have given the public the impression that this was only a lot of idle gossip being spread around by the Liberals.
Mr. Speaker, we have heard about these Government cutbacks and jobs ever since they came to power. According to their Budget, 15,000 jobs will be cut between now and 199091, and not long ago, we were told that in departments like the Department of Transport, an estimated 5,000 employees might be laid off.

The Department of External Affairs is to eliminate 182 positions this year". And I could go on, Mr. Speaker. I could tell you that at the Department of the Secretary of State, it seems 329 positions will be abolished. Several agencies, several Crown corporations have implemented one of this Government's policies, which is to reduce their establishment.
The Minister says that the Hon. Member is spreading false rumours! I wish the Parliamentary Secretary would at least confirm what the Minister said. It is true! He said: "We want the 1,500 jobs and more for Indian people, not federal bureaucrats". I am not here to criticize the Minister or to suggest what he should do, and whether his department should cut jobs to improve the services this Government is supposed to provide to our native peoples. It is not up to me to criticize the Government's policy to decentralize. I believe it is a good thing, but when they say we are spreading false rumours when we are only repeating what the Minister told us in the House, that is cutting it a bit fine.
Mr. Speaker, in last May's budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) himself announced that he intended to cut 15,000 jobs in the Public Service of Canada between now and 1990-91.
I repeat, the way this Government is hurrying to cut back human resources in the public service and agencies and Crown corporations, you would think they are trying to achieve in one or two years the goals they are supposed to attain in four or five, to make the Public Service more effective and efficient.

We were told that this would be done by attrition. At the time of the 1979 Government of a former Prime Minister, attrition was a buzz word. It was the gimmick used to tell people that the Government would cut into the Public Service of Canada and that no one would be affected. Attrition works sometimes, but it does not work all the time.
Adjournment Debate
I should not make an allusion to who is present in the House, but I see an Hon. Member across the way who knows what I am talking about. Attrition is the wrong tool to utilize when trying to make the Public Service more efficient and more effective. The attrition which we are told would be put into effect in this new program of 15,000 job cuts was indeed targeted to reduce x number of jobs in Departments. Months ago I asked the Government to come clean with the directives as to where, what and who would be affected. I have yet to receive a satisfactory answer on the objectives of the Government with regard to cutting the Public Service of Canada.
The most simple-minded individual would tell us that attrition, if used as a tool, will not work. We know that. We cannot replace an engineer with a technician. We cannot replace a meat inspector with someone doing clerical work in a level below the inspector. We cannot possibly use attrition to cut back in the Public Service. That has been proven in practice. It is not a good and efficient manner by which to cut into the Public Service.
In my opinion greater efficiency and effectiveness would be reached if we could consider and discuss here on the floor of this House the policies this Government wants to put into effect to make the Public Service more efficient and more effective. We will get savings by more efficiency; we will get possibly better results and better services by having more effective use of the people presently in the Public Service. We must remember that we have one of the best public services in the world and we must maintain it. We must not continue to spread the fear and the anxiety that these programs are creating amongst public servants.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) is committed to the principles of self-government for native people. In order to achieve this, the Department must transfer programs to Indian and Inuit people, a process which will involve careful planning and consultation. One of the major effects of such a transfer of programs is a down- sizing of the bureaucracy. The Minister is certainly concerned about the affected employees and will ensure that the impacts on them are minimized.
Departmental officials have begun the process of briefing employees, as well as continuing the consultation process with Indian organizations and chiefs across the country. Given the diverse nature of the Department, this process will take some time, but all employees will be made aware of the plan for reorganization.
The cornerstones of this new initiative have been articulated by the Minister. Each of these will have as its central theme programs and policies which respect the dignity and the way of life of Canada's Indian and Inuit peoples.

October 7, 1985
Adjournment Debate
The Department has been transferring programs to bands for a number of years and has been handling the resultant work force adjustment I think reasonably well. The Minister is calling for a redoubling of efforts within the Department to ensure that all reasonable efforts are made to meet the needs of those affected individuals.
Foremost will be the efforts by the Department to avoid laying off employees. The Department, through human resource planning, will ensure that normal attrition, a word which my colleague likes, and retirements are used to redeploy vulnerable employees into jobs which will not be affected by the down-sizing. These plans and all resourcing for the Department will be tightly controlled, and they will be monitored, if retraining is required for redeployment it will be provided, I assure you.
Eventually some employees will be given notices that they will be surplus. I wish to assure the Hon. Member and the House that every effort will be made to ensure that these employees have continuing employment. In the past many departmental employees have been hired by the bands or Indian organizations, and the Department has established policies which allow bands to set up pension plans reciprocal with those in the federal Government.
Other employees will choose continuing employment in the federal Government. The Department has set up a special work force adjustment unit which controls staffing at a departmental level and ensures fair consideration of surplus staff. The unit provides professional counselling services, helps establish retraining plans and works to meet the needs of individuals affected by changes in the Department.
Mr. Speaker, the Department has led the way in affording employees longer notice than was necessary under the administrative rules of the past Government. The Department gives at least six months notice of surplus to employees.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is concerned. He is concerned about ensuring that Indian people manage the programs which affect their communities. As a result of this initiative the Department will have to down-size, but it will be done in partnership with the Indian people of Canada, with concern for the individual needs of employees and in a manner which minimizes the impact on departmental employees. It will be done in accordance with a timetable that will be developed with the Indian people of Canada. When this timetable is established, the Minister will be in a better position to inform the House about the number of employees affected and the details of special programs to ensure that their needs are met.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-AIRLINE TICKET TAXES-EFFECT ON NORTHERN TRAVELLERS
AIR TRANSPORT-AIRLINE TICKET TAXES-EFFECT ON NORTHERN TRAVELLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by Order in Council P.C. 1985-2026 dated June 20, 1985, the cap or ceiling of $30 previously applied to the 9 per cent airline ticket tax was removed. In my question to the Acting Minister of Transport put on October 3, 1985, just a few days ago, I
pointed out how this was unfair to and discriminatory against northern air travellers.
I am not suggesting that members of the Cabinet, when they sat to discuss that Order in Council, passed it maliciously. I suspect it was an oversight on their part. They were looking at ways to raise additional revenue, in this case about $90 million Canada-wide, and they just did not consider the ramifications for the remote areas of the country. This points out the difficulties that occur when these things are done without proper parliamentary debate. When things are done through Order in Council, all the arguments cannot be brought to bear and things slip by. I would hope, Sir, that as a result of my presentation tonight the Government will change its policy.
In the North, there is very often no alternative but to fly. In a great many places there are no roads, and distances between sizeable communities are much greater than in the south. Per-mile costs are very much higher than in the south. They range from 10 per cent to more than 100 per cent higher. As well, it would appear that unless some changes in policy are to be made, the North is to be denied the full benefits of deregulation. The deregulation process is carrying on quite well in the south but whether or not it will be applied in its entirety to the North yet remains to be seen.
At the same time as this additional tax burden was placed on northerners, we see that literally hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent on transportation subsidies in the south. We need only look at the amount of money being given to Via Rail, for instance, none of which is of any advantage to northern travellers because we do not have Via Rail in that part of the country. I would hope that the policy being pursued is not to subsidize transportation in the south while applying the user-pay concept in the North.
In certain circumstances there has been an increase of up to tenfold in lease and rental fees being charged at the new air terminals in Whitehorse and Inuvik. Fees have been levied to such an extent that operators are not able to use the new facilities.
You will undoubtedly recall, Mr. Speaker, the recommendation of the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission which reported on the adequacy of air services in northern and remote areas in December of last year. The recommendation made as a result of a detailed study by the Air Transport Committee was the very reverse of that brought about by the Government. The commission's recommendation was that the air transport tax in the North be eliminated, quite the reverse of what really happened.
Let us take a look at some typical air fares. In the south, travelling from Toronto to Vancouver, a distance of 4,200 kilometres, costs $842 on a basic fare, and that brings about a tax of $76. In the North, the typical route of Yellowknife to Frobisher Bay, 2,900 kilometres, costs $1,488 on a basic fare, about twice as much per kilometre as in the south, and this would result in a tax of $134, about a 350 per cent increase in the tax previously levied when a cap was in place. At the same time, the tax on international flights has remained at only $15. How are we to encourage tourism in our own country and
October 7, 1985

particularly in northern and remote parts, when there is this discriminatory tax?
If you lived in Vancouver, Sir, you could fly to Hawaii on a special seat sale fare by spending just about the same amount of money you would pay in taxes to go from Vancouver to Frobisher Bay. That really does not encourage tourism. In the North perhaps 75 per cent to 80 per cent of air travellers are Government sponsored. They are either public servants flying around the country, or people involved with native organizations which are funded by Government. Perhaps they are people travelling for medical reasons, again, at public expense. Thus, in those cases, it is just taxpayers' money being shuffled from one pocket to the other.
This leaves a small number of people such as local business people and tourists who have to bear the brunt of this increase in taxation. That is hardly fair. This measure puts a disproportionate amount of hardship on northerners. I hope the Government will reconsider this matter, and take into account the advice of the Air Transport Committee and its recommendations. I hope the wide-ranging advice which has been received from all types of northern organizations, whether they be municipalities, chambers of commerce, organizations designed to promote tourism, or Ministers of Transport and Ministers of Finance will be taken into consideration. I hope that the cap will be placed back on in the case of northern transportation or, preferably, that the tax will be removed altogether.

I appreciate the remarks of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). As he knows, the Standing Committee on Transport will have an opportunity to travel to the North. I am sure the
Adjournment Debate
Minister would want me to invite the Hon. Member along on that trip. Indeed, I am sure he would want me to invite all Members from the North to make their views clearly known.
The air transportation tax is the one method by which we help pay for airport facilities and air navigation requirements and needs. As I have just mentioned, the deficit is some $778 million in this regard. That works out to about $58 for each round trip, which is a great deal of money. I was shocked and surprised to learn just how high the formula could take this amount in the North.
The change in tax will shift more of this burden to those who benefit directly. Not very many of us from the south fly in the North, just as I appreciate not very many northerners have access to VIA Rail. The federal Government has given special attention to the development of airport facilities and air navigation aids in the North because, as I have mentioned, it is of concern. There is a general exemption from the air transportation tax for all air travel on aircraft weighing less than 18,000 pounds. My distinguished colleague is aware of that. He may not be aware of the following. It is established that as many as 35,000 Arctic trips annually may benefit from this provision on at least part of their journey, if not the entirety.
Since 1979, smaller Arctic airports have been exempted from landing fees, aircraft parking fees and fuel concession fees, points so ably made by the Hon. Member. With respect to the larger airports and larger aircraft, the points he makes are substantial and true. However, landing fees have only been increased once since 1957 and they still remain approximately 60 per cent lower in the North than they are here in the south.
I reiterate to my distinguished colleague the pending presence in the North of the Standing Committee on Transport. I invite and urge him to make sure that his views are made clear and well known to the members of that committee.
